nodes.name: every G-module is a quotient of an induced module
nodes.statement:
We know (15), p. 62, that every $G$-module $M$ is a submodule of an induced module. It is also a quotient of an induced $G$-module because, on tensoring the augmentation sequence (19) with $M$, we obtain an exact sequence of $G$-modules

$$
0 \rightarrow M^{\prime} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} M \rightarrow M \rightarrow 0 .
$$
conclusions: every $G$-module $M$ is a submodule of an induced module
It is also a quotient of an induced $G$-module

nodes.name: extension of Res, Cor and Shapiro to Tate groups
nodes.statement:
This allows us to prove results by dimension shifting in both directions. Using this, it is possible to extend to all $r$, most of the results we proved for the groups $H^{r}(G, M)$ with $r \geq 0$. For example, Shapiro's lemma and its consequences are true, and the restriction and corestriction maps we defined in (1.27) and (1.29) extend to all the Tate cohomology groups. Specifically, there are canonical homomorphisms: ${ }^{4}$\\
Res: $H_{T}^{r}(G, M) \rightarrow H_{T}^{r}(H, M) \quad(H$ a subgroup of $G) ;$\\
Cor: $H_{T}^{r}(H, M) \rightarrow H_{T}^{r}(G, M) \quad(H$ a subgroup of $G)$.\\
Moreover, there is a natural action of $G / H$ on $H_{T}^{r}(H, M)$ for all $r \in \mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: By dimension shifting both ways, Shapiro's lemma, Res, Cor and the G/H-action extend to all Tate groups.

nodes.name: |G| kills Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: The composite Res ○ Cor is still multiplication by ( $G: H$ ). As $H_{T}^{r}(\{1\}, M)=0$ for all $r$, the argument in the proof of (1.30) shows that $H_{T}^{r}(G, M)$ is killed by $|G|$ for all $r$.
conclusions: $H_{T}^{r}(G, M)$ is killed by $|G|$ for all $r$

nodes.name: H_T^{-2}(G,Z) = G/G^c
nodes.statement:
Note that

$$
H_{T}^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z})=H_{1}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \simeq G / G^{c} .
$$

nodes.name: Proposition 3.2 (Cor and Res on H_T^{-2}; Verlagerung)
nodes.statement:
Proposition 3.2 Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.

\begin{itemize}
  \item[(a)] The map Cor: $H_{T}^{-2}(H, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H_{T}^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z})$ corresponds to the map $H / H^{c} \rightarrow G / G^{c}$ induced by the inclusion $H \hookrightarrow G$.
  \item[(b)] The map Res: $H_{T}^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H_{T}^{-2}(H, \mathbb{Z})$ corresponds to the Verlagerung map $G / G^{c} \rightarrow$ $H / H^{c}(V, 3.18)$.
nodes.statement_short: On H_T^{-2}(-,Z) = abelianization, Cor is induced by inclusion and Res is the transfer (Verlagerung).

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.2 (reference)
nodes.statement: Proof. See Weiss 1969, 3-5-5, 3-5-7. I'll include the proof in a future version of the notes. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Reference to Weiss 1969.

nodes.name: complete resolution computes Tate cohomology
nodes.statement:
There is a uniform explicit description of all the groups $H_{T}^{r}(G, M)$. In fact, there is an explicit complex $L_{\bullet}$ of $G$-modules (infinite in both directions) such that

$$
H_{T}^{r}(G, M)=H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{G}\left(L_{\bullet}, M\right)\right) .
$$

For $r>0$ this leads directly to the description we gave above of $H^{r}(G, M)$ in terms of inhomogeneous cocycles and coboundaries. See Weiss 1969, Chapter I.

nodes.name: cup-products on Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: When the group $G$ is finite, the cup-products extend in a unique way to all the cohomology groups, and have the same list of properties. See Weiss 1969, Chapter IV.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.3 (Tate cohomology of Q, Z)
nodes.section: The cohomology of finite cyclic groups

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement:
Proof. (a) The group $\mathbb{Q}$ is uniquely divisible, i.e., for all nonzero integers $m$, multiplication by $m: \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ is an isomorphism. Therefore the map $H_{T}^{r}(m): H_{T}^{r}(G, \mathbb{Q}) \rightarrow$ $H_{T}^{r}(G, \mathbb{Q})$, which is also multiplication by $m$, is an isomorphism. When we take $m=$ $(G: 1)$, we find that multiplication by $m$ on $H_{T}^{r}(G, \mathbb{Q})$ is both zero (see 1.30) and an isomorphism, which is possible only if $H_{T}^{r}(G, \mathbb{Q})=0$.\\
(b) Because $G$ acts trivially on $\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}^{G}=\mathbb{Z}$ and the norm map is multiplication by $(G: 1)$. Hence $H_{T}^{0}(G, \mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z} /(G: 1) \mathbb{Z}$. Moreover, $H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Z})=\operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z})$ (see 1.18a), but, because $\mathbb{Z}$ is torsion-free, all homomorphisms $G \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ are zero.\\
(c) The cohomology sequence of

$$
0 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0
$$

is an exact sequence\\

nodes.name: Tate groups H_T^0, H_T^{-1} of a cyclic group
nodes.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite cyclic group of order $m$, with generator $\sigma$. Then, by definition,

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_{T}^{0}(G, M) & =\frac{\operatorname{Ker}(\sigma-1)}{\operatorname{Im}\left(\mathrm{Nm}_{G}\right)} \\
H_{T}^{-1}(G, M) & =\frac{\operatorname{Ker}\left(\mathrm{Nm}_{G}\right)}{\operatorname{Im}(\sigma-1)} .
\end{aligned}
$$
nodes.section: The cohomology of finite cyclic groups

nodes.name: Proposition 3.4 (periodicity for cyclic groups)
nodes.statement:
Proposition 3.4 Let $G$ be a cyclic group of finite order. The choice of a generator for $G$ determines isomorphisms

$$
H_{T}^{r}(G, M) \xrightarrow{\simeq} H_{T}^{r+2}(G, M)
$$

for all $G$-modules $M$ and all $r \in \mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: The cohomology of finite cyclic groups
nodes.statement_short: For G finite cyclic, a generator gives isomorphisms H_T^r(G,M) = H_T^{r+2}(G,M).
assumptions: $G$ be a cyclic group of finite order
conclusions: The choice of a generator for $G$ determines isomorphisms

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4
nodes.statement:
Proof. Let $\sigma$ generate $G$. Then the sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{m \mapsto \sum_{g \in G} g m} \mathbb{Z}[G] \xrightarrow{\sigma-1} \mathbb{Z}[G] \xrightarrow{\sigma^{i} \mapsto 1} \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0
$$

is exact. Because the groups in the sequence and the kernel $I_{G}$ of $\mathbb{Z}[G] \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ are free $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, the sequence remains exact after it is tensored with $M$. Thus

$$
0 \rightarrow M \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} M \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} M \rightarrow M \rightarrow 0
$$

is an exact sequence of $G$-modules. Recall (1.4) that $\mathbb{Z}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} M \approx \mathbb{Z}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} M_{0}$, where $M_{0}$ is $M$ regarded as abelian group, and so $H_{T}^{r}\left(G, \mathbb{Z}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} M\right)=0$ for all $r$ by (3.1). Therefore (see 1.13), the sequence defines isomorphisms

$$
H_{T}^{r}(G, M) \xrightarrow{\simeq} H_{T}^{r+2}(G, M)
$$

for all $r$. \(\square\)

nodes.statement_short: Tensor the 4-term exact sequence 0 -> Z -> Z[G] -> Z[G] -> Z -> 0 with M; the middle terms are induced, so double dimension shift.

nodes.name: Remark 3.5 (periodicity is cup product with gamma)
nodes.statement: REMARK 3.5 Let $\gamma$ be the element of $H^{2}(G, \mathbb{Z})$ corresponding under the isomorphism $H^{2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})$ to the map sending the chosen generator $\sigma$ of $G$ to $1 / m$. Then the map $H_{T}^{r}(G, M) \rightarrow H_{T}^{r+2}(G, M)$ is $x \mapsto x \cup \gamma$. In a future version, I'll prove this. Serre, Local Fields, VIII, Section 4 gives the following hint: "the period isomorphisms are given by cup product with $\gamma$ : this follows, for example, from the formulas for the cup product given in Cartan-Eilenberg (Homological Algebra) p. 252." Alternatively, see Weiss 1969, 4-5-10.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient h(M)
nodes.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite cyclic group, and let $M$ be a $G$-module. When the cohomology groups $H^{r}(G, M)$ are finite, we define the Herbrand quotient of $M$ to be

$$
h(M)=\frac{\left|H_{T}^{0}(G, M)\right|}{\left|H_{T}^{1}(G, M)\right|} .
$$
nodes.section: The cohomology of finite cyclic groups

nodes.name: Proposition 3.6 (Herbrand quotient is multiplicative)
nodes.statement:
Proposition 3.6 Let $0 \rightarrow M^{\prime} \rightarrow M \rightarrow M^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow 0$ be an exact sequence of $G$-modules. If any two of the Herbrand quotients $h\left(M^{\prime}\right), h(M), h\left(M^{\prime \prime}\right)$ are defined, then so also is the third, and

$$
h(M)=h\left(M^{\prime}\right) h\left(M^{\prime \prime}\right) .
$$
nodes.section: The cohomology of finite cyclic groups
assumptions: $0 \rightarrow M^{\prime} \rightarrow M \rightarrow M^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow 0$ be an exact sequence of $G$-modules
any two of the Herbrand quotients $h\left(M^{\prime}\right), h(M), h\left(M^{\prime \prime}\right)$ are defined

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.6
nodes.statement:
Proof. We can truncate the (very) long exact cohomology sequence as follows,

$$
0 \rightarrow K \rightarrow H_{T}^{0}\left(M^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow H_{T}^{0}(M) \rightarrow H_{T}^{0}\left(M^{\prime \prime}\right) \rightarrow H^{1}\left(M^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow H^{1}(M) \rightarrow H^{1}\left(M^{\prime \prime}\right) \rightarrow K^{\prime} \rightarrow 0,
$$

where

$$
K=\operatorname{Coker}\left(H_{T}^{-1}(M) \rightarrow H_{T}^{-1}\left(M^{\prime \prime}\right)\right) \approx \operatorname{Coker}\left(H^{1}(M) \rightarrow H^{1}\left(M^{\prime \prime}\right)\right)=K^{\prime} .
$$

The first statement is now obvious, and the second follows from the next lemma. \(\square\)
nodes.section: The cohomology of finite cyclic groups
nodes.statement_short: Truncate the long exact sequence into a finite exact hexagon using periodicity; apply Lemma 3.7.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.7 (alternating product of orders)
nodes.statement:
Lemma 3.7 Let

$$
0 \rightarrow A_{0} \rightarrow A_{1} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow A_{r} \rightarrow 0
$$

be a exact sequence of finite groups. Then

$$
\frac{\left|A_{0}\right| \cdot\left|A_{2}\right| \cdots}{\left|A_{1}\right| \cdot\left|A_{3}\right| \cdots}=1 .
$$
nodes.section: The cohomology of finite cyclic groups
assumptions: be a exact sequence of finite groups

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.7
nodes.statement:
Proof. For a short exact sequence, that is, $r=2$, this is obvious, but every exact sequence can be broken up into short exact sequences,

$$
\begin{gathered}
0 \rightarrow A_{0} \rightarrow A_{1} \rightarrow C_{1} \rightarrow 0 \\
0 \rightarrow C_{1} \rightarrow A_{2} \rightarrow C_{2} \rightarrow 0 \\
\ldots \\
0 \rightarrow C_{r-1} \rightarrow A_{r-1} \rightarrow A_{r} \rightarrow 0
\end{gathered}
$$

Here $C_{i}=\operatorname{Coker}\left(A_{i-1} \rightarrow A_{i}\right)=\operatorname{Ker}\left(A_{i+1} \rightarrow A_{i+2}\right)$. From these sequences we find that

$$
1=\frac{\left|A_{0}\right| \cdot\left|C_{1}\right|}{\left|A_{1}\right|}=\frac{\left|A_{0}\right| \cdot\left|A_{2}\right|}{\left|A_{1}\right| \cdot\left|C_{2}\right|}=\cdots .
$$ \(\square\)

nodes.statement_short: Break into short exact sequences.

nodes.name: reduction
nodes.statement:
For a short exact sequence, that is, $r=2$, this is obvious, but every exact sequence can be broken up into short exact sequences,

$$
\begin{gathered}
0 \rightarrow A_{0} \rightarrow A_{1} \rightarrow C_{1} \rightarrow 0 \\
0 \rightarrow C_{1} \rightarrow A_{2} \rightarrow C_{2} \rightarrow 0 \\
\ldots \\
0 \rightarrow C_{r-1} \rightarrow A_{r-1} \rightarrow A_{r} \rightarrow 0
\end{gathered}
$$

nodes.statement_short: Obvious for short sequences; break up the long sequence

nodes.statement_short: Combine the identities for the short sequences

nodes.name: Proposition 3.8 (finite modules have h = 1)
nodes.statement: Proposition 3.8 If $M$ is a finite module, then $h(M)=1$.
nodes.section: The cohomology of finite cyclic groups

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.8
nodes.statement:
Proof. Consider the exact sequences

$$
0 \rightarrow M^{G} \rightarrow M \xrightarrow{g-1} M \rightarrow M_{G} \rightarrow 0
$$

and

$$
0 \rightarrow H_{T}^{-1}(M) \rightarrow M_{G} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Nm}_{G}} M^{G} \rightarrow H_{T}^{0}(M) \rightarrow 0,
$$

where $g$ is any generator of $G$. From the first sequence we find that $M^{G}$ and $M_{G}$ have the same order, and then from the second that $H_{T}^{-1}(M)$ and $H_{T}^{0}(M)$ have the same order. \(\square\)
nodes.section: The cohomology of finite cyclic groups
nodes.statement_short: Compare orders in 0 -> M^G -> M -> M -> M_G -> 0 and the norm sequence.

nodes.name: Corollary 3.9 (h invariant under finite kernel/cokernel)
nodes.statement: Corollary 3.9 Let $\alpha: M \rightarrow N$ be a homomorphism of $G$-modules with finite kernel and cokernel. If either $h(M)$ or $h(N)$ is defined, then so also is the other, and they are equal.
nodes.section: The cohomology of finite cyclic groups
assumptions: $\alpha: M \rightarrow N$ be a homomorphism of $G$-modules with finite kernel and cokernel
conclusions: so also is the other, and they are equal

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.9
nodes.statement:
Proof. Suppose $h(N)$ is defined, and consider the exact sequences:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 0 \rightarrow \alpha(M) \rightarrow N \rightarrow \operatorname{Coker}(\alpha) \rightarrow 0 \\
& 0 \rightarrow \operatorname{Ker}(\alpha) \rightarrow M \rightarrow \alpha(M) \rightarrow 0
\end{aligned}
$$

From the first sequence, we find that $h(\alpha M)$ is defined and equals $h(N)$, and from the second sequence we find that $h(M)$ is defined and equals $h(\alpha M)$. \(\square\)

nodes.statement_short: Apply Propositions 3.6 and 3.8 to the image and kernel sequences.

nodes.name: Theorem 3.10 (vanishing criterion)
nodes.statement:
Theorem 3.10 Let $G$ be a finite group, and let $M$ be a $G$-module. If

$$
H^{1}(H, M)=0=H^{2}(H, M)
$$

for all subgroups $H$ of $G$, then $H_{T}^{r}(G, M)=0$ for all $r \in \mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: If H^1(H,M) = H^2(H,M) = 0 for all subgroups H of the finite group G, then all Tate groups of M vanish.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.10
nodes.statement:
Proof. If $G$ is cyclic, this follows from the periodicity of the cohomology.\\
Assume now that $G$ is solvable. We shall prove the theorem in this case by induction on the order of $G$.

Because $G$ is solvable, it contains a proper normal subgroup $H$ such that $G / H$ is cyclic. Because $H$ has order less than that of $G$, and the pair $(H, M)$ satisfies the hypotheses of the theorem, $H^{r}(H, M)=0$ for all $r$. Therefore (see 1.34), we have exact sequences


\begin{equation*}
0 \rightarrow H^{r}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right) \rightarrow H^{r}(G, M) \rightarrow H^{r}(H, M) \tag{*}
\end{equation*}


for all $r \geq 1$. Because $H^{1}(G, M)=0=H^{2}(G, M), H^{1}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right)=H^{2}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right)=$ 0 , and because $G / H$ is cyclic, this implies that $H^{r}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right)=0$ for all $r$. Therefore, the sequences $(*)$ show that $H^{r}(G, M)=0$ for all $r>0$. We next show that $H^{0}(G, M)=0$. Let $x \in M^{G}$. Because $H^{0}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right)=0$, there exists a $y \in M^{H}$ such that $\operatorname{Nm}_{G / H}(y)=x$, and because $H^{0}(H, M)=0$, there exists a $z \in M$ such that $\operatorname{Nm}_{H}(z)=y$. Now

$$
\operatorname{Nm}_{G}(z)=\left(\operatorname{Nm}_{G / H} \circ \operatorname{Nm}_{H}\right)(z)=x .
$$

Thus, we now know that $H^{r}(G, M)=0$ for all $r \geq 0$.\\
To proceed further, we use the exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow M^{\prime} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} M \rightarrow M \rightarrow 0
$$

obtained by tensoring the augmentation sequence (19) with $M$. Recall that

$$
\mathbb{Z}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} M \stackrel{1.4}{\simeq} \mathbb{Z}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} M_{0} \stackrel{1.3}{\simeq} \operatorname{Ind}^{G}\left(M_{0}\right)
$$

is induced, and so $H^{r}\left(H, \mathbb{Z}[G] \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} M\right)=0$ for all $r$ and all subgroups $H$ of $G$. Therefore,

$$
H^{r}(H, M) \simeq H^{r+1}\left(H, M^{\prime}\right)
$$

for all $r$ and all $H$. In particular, $M^{\prime}$ satisfies the hypotheses of the theorem, and so (by what we have proved) $H^{r}\left(G, M^{\prime}\right)=0$ for $r \geq 0$. In particular,

$$
0=H^{0}\left(G, M^{\prime}\right)=H^{-1}(G, M) .
$$

The argument, when repeated, gives that $H^{-2}(G, M)=0$, etc.. This proves the theorem when $G$ is solvable.

Now consider the case of an arbitrary finite group $G$. If $G$ and $M$ satisfy the hypotheses of the theorem, so also do $G_{p}$ and $M$, where $G_{p}$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup. Therefore $H^{r}\left(G_{p}, M\right)=0$ for all $r$ and $p$, and so (see 1.33), the $p$-primary component of $H^{r}(G, M)$ is zero for all $r$ and $p$. This implies that $H^{r}(G, M)=0$ for all $r$. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Cyclic by periodicity; solvable by induction on |G| via inflation-restriction and dimension shifting; general via Sylow subgroups.

nodes.name: Tate's theorem
nodes.statement:
Theorem 3.11 (Tate's theorem) Let $G$ be a finite group and let $C$ be a $G$-module. Suppose that for all subgroups $H$ of $G$ (including $H=G$ ),

\begin{itemize}
  \item[(a)] $H^{1}(H, C)=0$, and
  \item[(b)] $H^{2}(H, C)$ is a cyclic group of order equal to $(H: 1)$.
\end{itemize}

Then, for all $r$, there is an isomorphism

$$
H_{T}^{r}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H_{T}^{r+2}(G, C)
$$

depending only on the choice of a generator for $H^{2}(G, C)$.
nodes.statement_short: If H^1(H,C) = 0 and H^2(H,C) is cyclic of order |H| for all subgroups H, then H_T^r(G,Z) = H_T^{r+2}(G,C) for all r.
assumptions: $H^{2}(H, C)$ is a cyclic group of order equal to $(H: 1)$
conclusions: for all $r$, there is an isomorphism

nodes.name: Proof of Tate's theorem
nodes.statement:
Proof. Choose a generator $\gamma$ for $H^{2}(G, C)$. Because $\operatorname{Cor} \circ \operatorname{Res}=(G: H), \operatorname{Res}(\gamma)$ generates $H^{2}(H, C)$ for any subgroup $H$ of $G$.

Let $\varphi$ be a cocycle representing $\gamma$. Define $C(\varphi)$ to be the direct sum of $C$ with the free abelian group having as basis symbols $x_{\sigma}$, one for each $\sigma \in G, \sigma \neq 1$, and extend the action of $G$ on $C$ to an action on $C(\varphi)$ by setting

$$
\sigma x_{\tau}=x_{\sigma \tau}-x_{\sigma}+\varphi(\sigma, \tau) .
$$

The symbol " $x_{1}$ " is to be interpreted as $\varphi(1,1)$. This does define an action of $G$ on $C(\varphi)$ because

$$
\rho \sigma x_{\tau}=x_{\rho \sigma \tau}-x_{\rho \sigma}+\varphi(\rho \sigma, \tau),
$$

whereas

$$
\begin{aligned}
\rho\left(\sigma x_{\tau}\right) & =\rho\left(x_{\sigma \tau}-x_{\sigma}+\varphi(\sigma, \tau)\right) \\
& =x_{\rho \sigma \tau}-x_{\rho}+\varphi(\rho, \sigma \tau)-\left(x_{\rho \sigma}-x_{\rho}+\varphi(\rho, \sigma)\right)+\rho \varphi(\sigma, \tau) .
\end{aligned}
$$

These agree because $\varphi$ satisfies the cocycle condition

$$
\rho \varphi(\sigma, \tau)+\varphi(\rho, \sigma \tau)=\varphi(\rho \sigma, \tau)+\varphi(\rho, \sigma) .
$$

Note that $\varphi$ is the coboundary of the 1 -cochain $\sigma \mapsto x_{\sigma}$, and so $\gamma$ maps to zero in $H^{2}(G, C(\varphi))$. For this reason, $C(\varphi)$ is called the splitting module for $\gamma$.

We shall first show that the hypotheses imply that

$$
H^{1}(H, C(\varphi))=0=H^{2}(H, C(\varphi))
$$

for all subgroups $H$ of $G$.\\
Recall that we have an exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow I_{G} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}[G] \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0,
$$

where $I_{G}$ is the free abelian group with basis the elements $\sigma-1, \sigma \in G, \sigma \neq 1$ Because $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ is induced, $H^{r}(H, \mathbb{Z}[G])=0$ for all $r$, and so

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
H^{1}\left(H, I_{G}\right) & \simeq H^{0}(H, \mathbb{Z}) \simeq \mathbb{Z} /(H: 1) \mathbb{Z}, \\
H^{2}\left(H, I_{G}\right) & \simeq H^{1}(H, \mathbb{Z})=0
\end{array}
$$

Define $\alpha$ to be the additive map $C(\varphi) \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}[G]$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha(c) & =0 \text { for all } c \in C \\
\alpha\left(x_{\sigma}\right) & =\sigma-1 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Clearly,

$$
0 \rightarrow C \rightarrow C(\varphi) \xrightarrow{\alpha} I_{G} \rightarrow 0
$$

is an exact sequence of $G$-modules. Its cohomology sequence reads

$$
0 \rightarrow H^{1}(H, C(\varphi)) \rightarrow H^{1}\left(H, I_{G}\right) \rightarrow H^{2}(H, C) \xrightarrow{0} H^{2}(H, C(\varphi)) \rightarrow 0
$$

The zeros at the ends use that $H^{1}(H, C)=0$ and $H^{2}\left(H, I_{G}\right)=0$. The map $H^{2}(H, C) \rightarrow$ $H^{2}(H, C(\varphi))$ is zero because $H^{2}(H, C)$ is generated by $\operatorname{Res}(\gamma)$, and this maps to the restriction of the image of $\gamma$ in $H^{2}(G, C(\varphi))$, which is zero. Therefore, $H^{1}\left(H, I_{G}\right) \rightarrow$ $H^{2}(H, C)$ is onto, and hence is an isomorphism (because the two groups have the same order). Its kernel and cokernel, namely, $H^{1}(H, C(\varphi))$ and $H^{2}(H, C(\varphi))$, are therefore both zero

We deduce from the Theorem 3.10 that $H^{r}(H, C(\varphi))=0$ for all $r$. On splicing the two short exact sequences together, we obtain an exact sequence


\begin{equation*}
0 \rightarrow C \rightarrow C(\varphi) \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}[G] \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0 \tag{24}
\end{equation*}


with the property that $H^{r}(G, C(\varphi))=0=H^{r}(G, \mathbb{Z}[G])$ for all $r$. Therefore, the double boundary map is an isomorphism (1.13)

$$
H^{r}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H^{r+2}(G, C) .
$$ \(\square\)

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
H^{1}\left(H, I_{G}\right) & \simeq H^{0}(H, \mathbb{Z}) \simeq \mathbb{Z} /(H: 1) \mathbb{Z}, \\
H^{2}\left(H, I_{G}\right) & \simeq H^{1}(H, \mathbb{Z})=0
\end{array}
$$
nodes.statement_short: From the augmentation sequence: H^1(H,I_G) = Z/(H:1), H^2(H,I_G) = 0

nodes.name: map alpha
nodes.statement:
Define $\alpha$ to be the additive map $C(\varphi) \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}[G]$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha(c) & =0 \text { for all } c \in C \\
\alpha\left(x_{\sigma}\right) & =\sigma-1 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Clearly,

$$
0 \rightarrow C \rightarrow C(\varphi) \xrightarrow{\alpha} I_{G} \rightarrow 0
$$

is an exact sequence of $G$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: 0 -> C -> C(phi) -> I_G -> 0 is exact

nodes.name: cohomology sequence
nodes.statement:
Its cohomology sequence reads

$$
0 \rightarrow H^{1}(H, C(\varphi)) \rightarrow H^{1}\left(H, I_{G}\right) \rightarrow H^{2}(H, C) \xrightarrow{0} H^{2}(H, C(\varphi)) \rightarrow 0
$$

The zeros at the ends use that $H^{1}(H, C)=0$ and $H^{2}\left(H, I_{G}\right)=0$. The map $H^{2}(H, C) \rightarrow$ $H^{2}(H, C(\varphi))$ is zero because $H^{2}(H, C)$ is generated by $\operatorname{Res}(\gamma)$, and this maps to the restriction of the image of $\gamma$ in $H^{2}(G, C(\varphi))$, which is zero. Therefore, $H^{1}\left(H, I_{G}\right) \rightarrow$ $H^{2}(H, C)$ is onto, and hence is an isomorphism (because the two groups have the same order). Its kernel and cokernel, namely, $H^{1}(H, C(\varphi))$ and $H^{2}(H, C(\varphi))$, are therefore both zero
nodes.statement_short: The connecting map is an isomorphism of groups of equal order, so H^1, H^2 of C(phi) vanish

nodes.name: apply Theorem 3.10
nodes.statement: We deduce from the Theorem 3.10 that $H^{r}(H, C(\varphi))=0$ for all $r$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.10: C(phi) is cohomologically trivial

nodes.name: splice
nodes.statement_short: Splice to (24); double boundary map is the isomorphism (1.13)

nodes.name: (24) Tate sequence
nodes.statement: 0 \rightarrow C \rightarrow C(\varphi) \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}[G] \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0 \tag{24}

nodes.name: Remark 3.12 (twisted Tate isomorphism)
nodes.statement:
REMARK 3.12 If $M$ is a $G$-module such that $\operatorname{Tor}_{1}^{\mathbb{Z}}(M, C)=0$, for example, if either $M$ or $C$ is torsion-free as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, then one can tensor the above 4-term sequence with $M$ and obtain isomorphisms

$$
H_{T}^{r}(G, M) \rightarrow H_{T}^{r+2}(G, M \otimes C) .
$$

nodes.name: Remark 3.13 (Tate isomorphism is cup product)
nodes.statement: REMARK 3.13 The map $H_{T}^{r}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H_{T}^{r+2}(G, C)$ is cup-product with the chosen element $\gamma \in H^{2}(G, C)$.

nodes.name: Example 3.14 (local Artin map from Tate's theorem)
nodes.statement:
Example 3.14 Let $K$ be a local field. We shall prove that for any finite Galois extension $L$ of $K$ with Galois group $G, H^{2}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)$is cyclic of order $[L: K]$ with a canonical generator $u_{L / K}$. Since we know that $H^{1}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)=0$ (Hilbert's Theorem 90), Tate's theorem shows that cup-product with $u_{L / K}$ is an isomorphism

$$
G^{\mathrm{ab}}=H_{T}^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H_{T}^{0}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)=K^{\times} / \operatorname{Nm} L^{\times} .
$$

The inverse isomorphism $K^{\times} / \operatorname{Nm} L^{\times} \xrightarrow{\simeq} G^{\text {ab }}$ is the local Artin map. The global Artin map can be obtained by a similar argument.
nodes.statement_short: For L/K local Galois, Hilbert 90 and H^2 cyclic of order [L:K] make Tate's theorem give G^ab = K^x / Nm L^x, inverse to the local Artin map.

nodes.name: directed set
nodes.statement: A partially ordered set $(I, \leq)$ is said to be directed if for any two elements $i$ and $j$ of $I$, there exists a $k$ such that $i, j \leq k$.

nodes.name: direct system
direct limit
nodes.statement:
On the disjoint union $\coprod A_{i}$ of the $A_{i}$, introduce the equivalence relation under which $a_{i} \in A_{i}$ is related to $a_{j} \in A_{j}$ if and only if $\alpha_{k i}\left(a_{i}\right)=\alpha_{k j}\left(a_{j}\right)$ for some $k \geq i, j$. The corresponding quotient set is called the direct limit of the $A_{i}$ (relative to the $\alpha_{j i}$ ):

$$
A=\underset{\longrightarrow}{\lim } A_{i} .
$$

nodes.name: canonical maps to the direct limit
universal property of the direct limit
nodes.statement: The system ( $A, \alpha_{i}$ ) has the following universal property: let $T$ be a set and let ( $\beta_{i}$ ), $\beta_{i}: A_{i} \rightarrow T$, be a family of maps such that $\beta_{i}=\beta_{j} \circ \alpha_{j i}$ for $i \leq j$; then there exists a unique map $\beta: A \rightarrow T$ such that $\beta_{i}=\beta \circ \alpha_{i}$ for all $i$.

nodes.name: direct limit of abelian groups
nodes.statement: If the $A_{i}$ are abelian groups and the $\alpha_{i j}$ are homomorphisms, then $A$ has a unique structure of an abelian group for which the $\alpha_{i}$ are homomorphisms.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.1 (direct limits are exact)
nodes.statement:
Lemma 4.1 For any direct system of exact sequences

$$
A_{i} \rightarrow B_{i} \rightarrow C_{i},
$$

the sequence

$$
\xrightarrow{\lim } A_{i} \rightarrow \underset{\longrightarrow}{\lim } B_{i} \rightarrow \underset{\longrightarrow}{\lim } C_{i}
$$

is again exact. Therefore the formation of direct limits commutes with passage to cohomology in complexes.
conclusions: the formation of direct limits commutes with passage to cohomology in complexes

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: Proof. Exercise for the reader. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Left to the reader.

nodes.name: profinite group
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a profinite group. This means that $G$ is a compact ${ }^{5}$ topological group for which the open normal subgroups form a fundamental system of neighbourhoods of 1.
differentia: the open normal subgroups form a fundamental system of neighbourhoods of 1

nodes.name: discrete G-module
continuous cohomology H^r_cts(G,M)
nodes.statement:
The discrete $G$-modules form an abelian category with enough injectives, and so we can define cohomology groups $H_{\text {cts }}^{r}(G, M), r \geq 0$, by taking injective resolutions, just as before. Moreover, the groups can be calculated using continuous cocycles: for $r \geq 0$, let $C_{\text {cts }}^{r}(G, M)$ be the group of continuous maps $G^{r} \rightarrow M$, and define $d^{r}: C_{\text {cts }}^{r}(G, M) \rightarrow$ $C_{\text {cts }}^{r+1}(G, M)$ as before; then

$$
H_{\mathrm{cts}}^{r}(G, M)=\frac{Z_{\mathrm{cts}}^{r}(G, M)}{B_{\mathrm{cts}}^{r}(G, M)},
$$

where $Z_{\text {cts }}^{r}(G, M)=\operatorname{Ker}\left(d^{r}\right)$ and $B_{\text {cts }}^{r}(G, M)=\operatorname{Im}\left(d^{r-1}\right)$.

nodes.name: Argument for Proposition 4.2
nodes.statement:
Let $\varphi: G^{r} \rightarrow M$ be a continuous $r$-cochain. Then $\varphi\left(G^{r}\right)$ is compact (because $G^{r}$ is compact) and discrete (because $M$ is discrete), and so it is finite, and hence it is contained in $M^{H_{0}}$ for some open normal subgroup $H_{0}$ of $G$. The inverse image $\varphi^{-1}(m)$ of each point $m$ of $\varphi\left(G^{r}\right)$ is open, and so contains a translate of $H(m)^{r}$ for some open normal subgroup $H(m)$ of $G$. Let $H_{1}=\bigcap_{m \in \varphi\left(G^{r}\right)} H(m)$. ${ }^{6}$ This is again an open subgroup of $G$, and $\varphi$ factors through $\left(G / H_{1}\right)^{r}$. Let $H=H_{0} \cap H_{1}$. Then $\varphi$ arises by inflation from an $r$-cocycle on $G / H$ with values in $M^{H}$. In other words, the map

$$
\xrightarrow{\lim _{\longrightarrow}} C^{r}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right) \rightarrow C_{\mathrm{cts}}^{r}(G, M)
$$

is surjective. It is not difficult to see that it is also injective. Because passage to the direct limit commutes with the formation of kernels and cokernels, and hence with the formation of cohomology, we obtain the following proposition:
nodes.statement_short: A continuous cochain has finite image and factors through a finite quotient; so cochains are a direct limit, and direct limits commute with cohomology.

nodes.name: finite image
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi: G^{r} \rightarrow M$ be a continuous $r$-cochain. Then $\varphi\left(G^{r}\right)$ is compact (because $G^{r}$ is compact) and discrete (because $M$ is discrete), and so it is finite, and hence it is contained in $M^{H_{0}}$ for some open normal subgroup $H_{0}$ of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Compact image in a discrete module is finite

nodes.name: factors through quotient
nodes.statement: The inverse image $\varphi^{-1}(m)$ of each point $m$ of $\varphi\left(G^{r}\right)$ is open, and so contains a translate of $H(m)^{r}$ for some open normal subgroup $H(m)$ of $G$. Let $H_{1}=\bigcap_{m \in \varphi\left(G^{r}\right)} H(m)$. ${ }^{6}$ This is again an open subgroup of $G$, and $\varphi$ factors through $\left(G / H_{1}\right)^{r}$.
nodes.statement_short: phi is constant on cosets of an open normal subgroup

nodes.name: surjectivity
nodes.statement:
Let $H=H_{0} \cap H_{1}$. Then $\varphi$ arises by inflation from an $r$-cocycle on $G / H$ with values in $M^{H}$. In other words, the map

$$
\xrightarrow{\lim _{\longrightarrow}} C^{r}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right) \rightarrow C_{\mathrm{cts}}^{r}(G, M)
$$

is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: phi is inflated from G/H; the limit map on cochains is surjective

nodes.name: injectivity
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to see that it is also injective.
nodes.statement_short: and injective

nodes.name: limits commute
nodes.statement: Because passage to the direct limit commutes with the formation of kernels and cokernels, and hence with the formation of cohomology, we obtain the following proposition:
nodes.statement_short: Direct limits commute with cohomology

nodes.name: Proposition 4.2 (profinite cohomology as a direct limit)
nodes.statement:
Proposition 4.2 The maps $\operatorname{Inf}: H^{r}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right) \rightarrow H_{\text {cts }}^{r}(G, M)$ realize $H_{\text {cts }}^{r}(G, M)$ as the direct limit of the groups $H^{r}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right)$ as $H$ runs through the open normal subgroups $H$ of $G$ :

$$
\lim _{\longrightarrow} H^{r}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right)=H_{c t s}^{r}(G, M) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: H^r_cts(G,M) is the direct limit of H^r(G/H, M^H) over open normal subgroups H, via inflation.

nodes.name: Corollary 4.3 (profinite cohomology is torsion)
nodes.statement: Corollary 4.3 For every profinite group $G$ and discrete $G$-module $M, H^{r}(G, M)$ is a torsion group for all $r>0$.
conclusions: H^{r}(G, M)$ is a torsion group for all $r>0$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.3
nodes.statement: Proof. Each of the groups $H^{r}\left(G / H, M^{H}\right), r>0$, is torsion (see1.31). \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Each finite-level group is torsion by Corollary 1.31.

nodes.name: continuous cochain theory extends
nodes.statement: Most of the theory concerning the cohomology groups $H^{r}(G, M)$ for $r \geq 0$ continues to hold for the groups defined by continuous cochains. For example, if $H$ is a closed subgroup of $G$, there are maps Inf, Res, and Cor (the last requires $H$ to be of finite index), and there are cup-product maps.

nodes.name: Proposition 4.4 (cohomology commutes with direct limits)
nodes.statement: Proposition 4.4 Let $G$ be a profinite group, and let $M$ be a discrete $G$-module. If $M=$ $\xrightarrow{\lim } M_{i}$, where $M_{i} \subset M$, then $H^{r}(G, M)=\underset{\longrightarrow}{\lim } H^{r}\left(G, M_{i}\right)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.4
nodes.statement:
Proof. Because $G$ is compact and $M$ is discrete, the image of any $r$-cochain $f: G^{r} \rightarrow M$ is finite. Since the $M_{i}$ form a directed system of submodules of $M$ (i.e., given $M_{i}$ and $M_{j}$, there is an $M_{k}$ containing both of them) and $M=\bigcup M_{i}$, every finite subset of $M$ is contained in an $M_{i}$. It follows that $C^{r}(G, M)=\underset{\longrightarrow}{\lim } C^{r}\left(G, M_{i}\right)$, and so Lemma 4.1 shows that

$$
H^{r}\left(C^{\bullet}(G, M)\right)=\underset{\longrightarrow}{\lim } H^{r}\left(C^{\bullet}\left(G, M_{i}\right)\right) .
$$ \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Cochains have finite image, hence land in some M_i; so cochains form a direct limit and Lemma 4.1 applies.

nodes.name: finite image
nodes.statement: Because $G$ is compact and $M$ is discrete, the image of any $r$-cochain $f: G^{r} \rightarrow M$ is finite.
nodes.statement_short: Cochains have finite image

nodes.name: finite subsets in some M_i
nodes.statement: Since the $M_{i}$ form a directed system of submodules of $M$ (i.e., given $M_{i}$ and $M_{j}$, there is an $M_{k}$ containing both of them) and $M=\bigcup M_{i}$, every finite subset of $M$ is contained in an $M_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Finite subsets lie in some M_i

nodes.name: apply Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement:
It follows that $C^{r}(G, M)=\underset{\longrightarrow}{\lim } C^{r}\left(G, M_{i}\right)$, and so Lemma 4.1 shows that

$$
H^{r}\left(C^{\bullet}(G, M)\right)=\underset{\longrightarrow}{\lim } H^{r}\left(C^{\bullet}\left(G, M_{i}\right)\right) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: Cochains are a direct limit; apply Lemma 4.1

nodes.name: Aside 4.5 (discrete vs all G-modules)
nodes.statement:
Aside 4.5 (For the experts.) Let $G$ be a profinite group, let $\mathrm{M}(G)$ be the category of all $G$-modules, and $\mathrm{C}(G)$ the category of discrete $G$-modules. Then $\mathrm{C}(G)$ is a full subcategory of $\mathrm{M}(G)$. Moreover, there is a functor

$$
M \mapsto M^{*} \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \bigcup_{H \text { open in } G} M^{H}: \mathrm{M}(G) \rightarrow \mathrm{C}(G) .
$$

Clearly,

$$
\operatorname{Hom}_{G}\left(M, N^{*}\right)=\operatorname{Hom}_{G}(M, N)
$$

for $M$ a discrete $G$-module. The inclusion functor $i: \mathrm{C}(G) \rightarrow \mathrm{M}(G)$ is exact, but doesn't preserve injectives-hence $H^{r}(G, M) \neq H^{r}(G, i M)$ in general. On the other hand, $M \mapsto M^{*}$ preserves injectives, but is only left exact-hence $\mathrm{C}(M)$ has enough injectives. Again $H^{r}(G, M) \neq$ $H^{r}\left(G, M^{*}\right)$ (however, there is a spectral sequence ...).

nodes.name: The Extended Snake Lemma
nodes.statement: Lemma A. 1 (The Extended Snake Lemma) The exact commutative diagram in blue gives rise to the exact sequence in red:
nodes.origin_citation: snake lemma, standard; after F. Lemmermeyer, The Snake Lemma

nodes.name: Proof of the Extended Snake Lemma
nodes.statement: Proof. Except for the first and last terms, this is standard. A small diagram chase shows that $\operatorname{Ker} f \subset \operatorname{Ker}(a)$, from which exactness at $\operatorname{Ker} a$ follows. The proof of exactness at Coker $c$ is similarly straightforward. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Standard except the end terms, which follow by small diagram chases.

nodes.name: standard part
nodes.statement: Except for the first and last terms, this is standard.
nodes.statement_short: The middle is the usual snake lemma

nodes.name: end terms
nodes.statement: A small diagram chase shows that $\operatorname{Ker} f \subset \operatorname{Ker}(a)$, from which exactness at $\operatorname{Ker} a$ follows. The proof of exactness at Coker $c$ is similarly straightforward.
nodes.statement_short: Diagram chases give exactness at Ker a and Coker c

nodes.name: Kernel-Cokernel Lemma
nodes.statement:
Lemma A. 2 (Kernel-Cokernel Lemma) Every pair of homomorphisms

$$
A \xrightarrow{f} B \xrightarrow{g} C
$$

of abelian groups gives rise to an exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow \operatorname{Ker} f \rightarrow \operatorname{Ker} g \circ f \xrightarrow{f} \operatorname{Ker} g \rightarrow \operatorname{Coker} f \rightarrow \operatorname{Coker} g \circ f \rightarrow \operatorname{Coker} g \rightarrow 0 .
$$
conclusions: gives rise to an exact sequence

nodes.name: Proof of the Kernel-Cokernel Lemma
nodes.statement:
Proof. Apply the extended snake lemma to\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-34_193_768_424_639} \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Apply the extended snake lemma to a suitable diagram.

nodes.name: category
covariant functor
nodes.statement: A covariant functor $F: \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{D}$ is a "map" that attaches to each object $A$ of C an object $F(A)$ of D and to each morphism $\alpha: A \rightarrow B$ a morphism $F(\alpha): F(A) \rightarrow F(B)$ such that $F(\alpha \circ \beta)=F(\alpha) \circ F(\beta)$ and $F\left(\operatorname{id}_{A}\right)=\operatorname{id}_{F(A)}$.

nodes.name: left adjoint
nodes.statement:
A functor $F: \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{D}$ is left adjoint to the functor $G: \mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}$ if there is a natural isomorphism

$$
\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(F(A), B) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{C}(A, G(B)) .
$$

nodes.name: additive category
nodes.statement: If the sets $\operatorname{Hom}(A, B)$ are endowed with the structures of abelian groups in such a way that the composition maps are bi-additive, and every finite collection of objects in C has a direct sum, then C (together with the structures) is called an additive category.

nodes.name: direct sum in an additive category
nodes.statement:
To say that $A$ and $B$ admit a direct sum means that there is an object $A \oplus B$ in C and maps $i_{A}: A \rightarrow A \oplus B$, $i_{B}: B \rightarrow A \oplus B, p_{A}: A \oplus B \rightarrow A, p_{B}: A \oplus B \rightarrow B$ such that:

$$
\begin{array}{cc}
p_{A} \circ i_{A}=\operatorname{id}_{A} & p_{B} \circ i_{B}=\operatorname{id}_{B} \\
p_{A} \circ i_{B}=0 & p_{B} \circ i_{A}=0 \\
& i_{A} p_{A}+i_{B} p_{B}=1_{A \oplus B} .
\end{array}
$$

nodes.name: exact sequence in an additive category
nodes.statement:
Let C be an additive category. A sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow A \rightarrow B \xrightarrow{\alpha} C
$$

is exact if the sequence of abelian groups

$$
0 \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(T, A) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(T, B) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(T, C)
$$

is exact for all objects $T$. A sequence

$$
A \xrightarrow{\beta} B \rightarrow C \rightarrow 0
$$

is exact if the sequence of abelian groups

$$
0 \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(C, T) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(B, T) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(A, T)
$$

is exact for all objects $T$.

nodes.name: kernel and cokernel
nodes.statement: When the first sequence is exact, $A$ is called the kernel of $\alpha$, and when the second is exact, $C$ is called the cokernel of $\beta$.

nodes.name: monomorphism
nodes.statement: A morphism $A \rightarrow B$ is said to be injective (or a monomorphism) if $0 \rightarrow A \rightarrow B$ is exact.

nodes.name: epimorphism
nodes.statement: Similarly, it is surjective (or an epimorphism) if $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow 0$ is exact.

nodes.name: image and coimage
nodes.statement: Let C be an additive category in which every morphism has both a kernel and a cokernel. Let $\alpha: A \rightarrow B$ be morphism. The kernel of the cokernel $B \rightarrow C$ of $\alpha$ is called the image of $\alpha$, and the cokernel of the kernel of $\alpha$ is called the coimage of $\alpha$.

nodes.name: abelian category
nodes.statement: There is a canonical map from the coimage of $\alpha$ to the image of $\alpha$, and if this is always an isomorphism, then C is called an abelian category.

nodes.name: additive functor
nodes.statement: Functors between additive categories will be assumed to be additive, i.e., such that the maps $\operatorname{Hom}(A, B) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(F(A), F(B))$ are homomorphisms of abelian groups.

nodes.name: exact functor
nodes.statement: Such a functor is said to be exact if it maps exact sequences to exact sequences.

nodes.name: injective object
nodes.statement:
Let C be an abelian category. An object $I$ of C is injective if $\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot, I)$ is an exact functor, i.e., if

$$
0 \rightarrow A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow 0
$$

exact in C implies that

$$
0 \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(C, I) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(B, I) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(A, I) \rightarrow 0
$$

is exact.

nodes.name: injectivity as extension property
nodes.statement:
The last sequence is automatically exact except at\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-35_206_185_1819_1451}\\
$\operatorname{Hom}(A, I)$, and so to say that $I$ is injective means that, whenever $A$ is a subobject of $B$, every homomorphism $A \rightarrow I$ extends to $B$.

nodes.name: enough injectives
nodes.statement: An abelian category C is said to have enough injectives if every object admits an injective homomorphism into an injective object.

nodes.name: Proposition A.3 (injective = divisible over a PID)
nodes.statement: Proposition A. 3 A module $M$ over a principal ideal domain $R$ is injective if and only if it is divisible, i.e., the map $x \mapsto r x$ is surjective for all $r \in R, r \neq 0$.
assumptions: A module $M$ over a principal ideal domain $R$
conclusions: is injective if and only if it is divisible

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.3
nodes.statement:
Proof. injective ⟹ divisible: Let $m \in M$ and let $r$ be a nonzero element of $R$. The map $x \mapsto r x: R \rightarrow R$ is injective, and every extension of $x \mapsto x m: R \rightarrow M$ to $R$ will send 1 to an element $m^{\prime}$ such that $r m^{\prime}=m$.\\
divisible ⇒ injective: Suppose that $M$ is divisible, and consider a homomorphism $\alpha: A \rightarrow M$, where $A$ is a submodule of $B$. On applying Zorn's lemma to the set of pairs

\footnotetext{${ }^{9}$ If you are mystified by this paragraph, you may find sx2263197 helpful.
}
( $A^{\prime}, \alpha^{\prime}$ ), where $A^{\prime}$ is a submodule of $B$ containing $A$ and $\alpha^{\prime}$ extends $\alpha$ to $A^{\prime}$, we obtain a maximal such pair $\left(A_{1}, \alpha_{1}\right)$. If $A_{1} \neq B$, then there exists a $b \in B \backslash A_{1}$, and we define $I=\left\{r \in R \mid r b \in A_{1}\right\}$. Because $M$ is divisible, the map $r \mapsto \alpha_{1}(r b): I \rightarrow M$ extends ${ }^{10}$ to $R$, but this implies that $\alpha_{1}$ extends to $A_{1}+R b$, which contradicts the maximality of $\left(A_{1}, \alpha_{1}\right)$. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Injective implies divisible by extending x -> xm from rR; divisible implies injective by Zorn's lemma on partial extensions.

nodes.name: injective implies divisible
nodes.statement: injective ⟹ divisible: Let $m \in M$ and let $r$ be a nonzero element of $R$. The map $x \mapsto r x: R \rightarrow R$ is injective, and every extension of $x \mapsto x m: R \rightarrow M$ to $R$ will send 1 to an element $m^{\prime}$ such that $r m^{\prime}=m$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the map from R to R through multiplication by r

nodes.name: divisible implies injective
nodes.statement:
divisible ⇒ injective: Suppose that $M$ is divisible, and consider a homomorphism $\alpha: A \rightarrow M$, where $A$ is a submodule of $B$. On applying Zorn's lemma to the set of pairs

\footnotetext{${ }^{9}$ If you are mystified by this paragraph, you may find sx2263197 helpful.
}
( $A^{\prime}, \alpha^{\prime}$ ), where $A^{\prime}$ is a submodule of $B$ containing $A$ and $\alpha^{\prime}$ extends $\alpha$ to $A^{\prime}$, we obtain a maximal such pair $\left(A_{1}, \alpha_{1}\right)$. If $A_{1} \neq B$, then there exists a $b \in B \backslash A_{1}$, and we define $I=\left\{r \in R \mid r b \in A_{1}\right\}$. Because $M$ is divisible, the map $r \mapsto \alpha_{1}(r b): I \rightarrow M$ extends ${ }^{10}$ to $R$, but this implies that $\alpha_{1}$ extends to $A_{1}+R b$, which contradicts the maximality of $\left(A_{1}, \alpha_{1}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Zorn's lemma and maximal extension

nodes.name: maximal extension
nodes.statement:
divisible ⇒ injective: Suppose that $M$ is divisible, and consider a homomorphism $\alpha: A \rightarrow M$, where $A$ is a submodule of $B$. On applying Zorn's lemma to the set of pairs

\footnotetext{${ }^{9}$ If you are mystified by this paragraph, you may find sx2263197 helpful.
}
( $A^{\prime}, \alpha^{\prime}$ ), where $A^{\prime}$ is a submodule of $B$ containing $A$ and $\alpha^{\prime}$ extends $\alpha$ to $A^{\prime}$, we obtain a maximal such pair $\left(A_{1}, \alpha_{1}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal extension (A_1, alpha_1)

nodes.name: extend further
nodes.statement: If $A_{1} \neq B$, then there exists a $b \in B \backslash A_{1}$, and we define $I=\left\{r \in R \mid r b \in A_{1}\right\}$. Because $M$ is divisible, the map $r \mapsto \alpha_{1}(r b): I \rightarrow M$ extends ${ }^{10}$ to $R$, but this implies that $\alpha_{1}$ extends to $A_{1}+R b$, which contradicts the maximality of $\left(A_{1}, \alpha_{1}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Divisibility extends past A_1, contradicting maximality

nodes.name: quotients of injectives over a PID; Q/Z injective
nodes.statement: Therefore, when $R$ is a principal ideal domain, every quotient of an injective module is injective, for example, $K / R$, where $K$ is the field of fractions of $R$. In particular, $\mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}$ is an injective abelian group.
conclusions: every quotient of an injective module is injective

nodes.name: Proposition A.4 (enough injectives over a PID)
nodes.statement: Proposition A. 4 The category of modules over a principal ideal domain $R$ has enough injectives.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.4
nodes.statement:
Proof. Write $M$ as a quotient $M \approx F / N$ of a free $R$-module $F$, and consider the exact commutative diagram,\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-36_173_951_1017_556}\\
Because $F \rightarrow F \otimes_{R} K$ is an injective map and $F \otimes_{R} K$ is an injective object, the map $M \rightarrow\left(F \otimes_{R} K\right) / N$ is an injective homomorphism of $M$ into an injective $R$-module. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Embed F/N into (F (x) K)/N, which is divisible hence injective.

nodes.name: Alternative proof of A.4 for abelian groups
nodes.statement: For abelian groups, the proposition can also be proved as follows: for an abelian group $M$, let $M^{\vee}=\operatorname{Hom}(M, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})$; choose a free abelian group $F$ mapping onto $M^{\vee}, F \rightarrow$ $M^{\vee}$; then $M \hookrightarrow M^{\vee \vee} \hookrightarrow F^{\vee}$, and $F^{\vee}$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: Embed M into the dual of a free group mapping onto its Q/Z-dual.

nodes.name: Proposition A.5 (right adjoints of exact functors preserve injectives)
nodes.statement: Proposition A. 5 A functor that admits an exact left adjoint preserves injectives.
assumptions: A functor that admits an exact left adjoint

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.5
nodes.statement: Proof. Let $F^{\prime}$ be an exact left adjoint to the functor $F: \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{D}$. For every injective object $I$ in C, the functor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{D}}(\cdot, F(I))$ is isomorphic to the functor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{C}}\left(F^{\prime}(\cdot), I\right)$, which is exact because it is the composite of two exact functors, namely, $F^{\prime}$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{C}}(\cdot, I)$. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Hom_D(-, F(I)) = Hom_C(F'(-), I) is a composite of exact functors.

nodes.name: resolution
nodes.statement:
Let $M$ be an object of C. A resolution of $M$ is a long exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow M \rightarrow I^{0} \xrightarrow{d^{0}} I^{1} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow I^{r} \xrightarrow{d^{r}} I^{r+1} \rightarrow \cdots .
$$

nodes.name: injective resolution
nodes.statement: If the $I^{r}$ 's are injective objects of C, then it is called an injective resolution. We sometimes denote this complex by $M \rightarrow I^{\bullet}$.

nodes.name: Lemma A.6 (injective resolutions exist and compare)
nodes.statement:
Lemma A. 6 An injective resolution $M \rightarrow I^{\bullet}$ of $M$ exists, and if $M \rightarrow J^{\bullet}$ is a second injective resolution, then there exists a homomorphism from $M \rightarrow I^{\bullet}$ to $M \rightarrow J^{\bullet}$, i.e., there exists a commutative diagram,\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-37_180_704_514_681}
nodes.statement_short: Injective resolutions exist, and any two are related by a morphism of resolutions.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.6
nodes.statement:
Proof. By assumption, there exists an injective morphism

$$
0 \rightarrow M \rightarrow I^{0}
$$

with $I^{0}$ injective. Let $B^{1}$ be the cokernel of the map. Again, there exists an injective morphism

$$
0 \rightarrow B^{1} \rightarrow I^{1}
$$

with $I^{1}$ injective. Now

$$
0 \rightarrow M \rightarrow I^{0} \rightarrow I^{1}
$$

is exact. Let $B^{2}=\operatorname{Coker}\left(B^{1} \rightarrow I^{1}\right)$, and continue in this fashion.\\
Similarly, a morphism of resolutions can be constructed step by step, using the definition of an injective object. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Build the resolution step by step by embedding successive cokernels in injectives; morphisms likewise.

nodes.name: first step
nodes.statement:
By assumption, there exists an injective morphism

$$
0 \rightarrow M \rightarrow I^{0}
$$

with $I^{0}$ injective.
nodes.statement_short: Embed M in an injective I^0

nodes.name: second step
nodes.statement:
Let $B^{1}$ be the cokernel of the map. Again, there exists an injective morphism

$$
0 \rightarrow B^{1} \rightarrow I^{1}
$$

with $I^{1}$ injective.
nodes.statement_short: Embed the cokernel B^1 in I^1

nodes.name: continue
nodes.statement:
Now

$$
0 \rightarrow M \rightarrow I^{0} \rightarrow I^{1}
$$

is exact. Let $B^{2}=\operatorname{Coker}\left(B^{1} \rightarrow I^{1}\right)$, and continue in this fashion.\\
Similarly, a morphism of resolutions can be constructed step by step, using the definition of an injective object.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate

nodes.name: cohomology of F(I^bullet)
nodes.statement:
On applying a left exact functor $F$ to an injective resolution $M \rightarrow I^{\bullet}$ of a object $M$, we obtain a complex

$$
F\left(I^{\bullet}\right): F\left(I^{0}\right) \rightarrow F\left(I^{1}\right) \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow F\left(I^{r}\right) \xrightarrow{F\left(d^{r}\right)} F\left(I^{r+1}\right) \rightarrow \cdots
$$

which may no longer be exact, and so the cohomology groups

$$
H^{r}\left(F\left(I^{\bullet}\right)\right) \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \frac{\operatorname{Ker}\left(F\left(d^{r}\right)\right)}{\operatorname{Im}\left(F\left(d^{r-1}\right)\right)}
$$

may be nonzero.

nodes.name: Remark A.7 (H^0 = F(M))
nodes.statement:
Remark A. 7 Because $F$ is left exact, the sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow F(M) \rightarrow F\left(I^{0}\right) \xrightarrow{d^{0}} F\left(I^{1}\right)
$$

is exact. Therefore,

$$
H^{0}\left(F\left(I^{\bullet}\right)\right) \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \operatorname{Ker}\left(d^{0}\right)=F(M) .
$$

nodes.name: Proposition A.8 (maps of resolutions are unique up to cohomology)
nodes.statement:
Proposition A. 8 Let $M \rightarrow I^{\bullet}$ and $N \rightarrow J^{\bullet}$ be injective resolutions of objects $M$ and $N$ of C. Every morphism $\alpha: M \rightarrow N$ extends to a map of complexes\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-37_170_241_2205_915}\\
For every left exact functor $F$, the morphism

$$
H^{r}\left(F\left(\alpha^{\bullet}\right)\right): H^{r}\left(F\left(I^{\bullet}\right)\right) \rightarrow H^{r}\left(F\left(J^{\bullet}\right)\right)
$$

is independent of the choice of $\alpha^{\bullet}$.
nodes.statement_short: Morphisms extend to injective resolutions, and the induced map on H^r(F(-)) is independent of the extension.

nodes.name: H^r(F(I^bullet)) well defined
nodes.statement: The proposition, applied to the identity morphism $M \rightarrow M$, implies that the objects $H^{r}\left(F\left(I^{\bullet}\right)\right)$ are well-defined up to a well-defined isomorphism: given two injective resolutions $M \rightarrow I^{\bullet}$ and $M \rightarrow J^{\bullet}$ of $M$, there exists a morphism $\alpha^{\bullet}: I^{\bullet} \rightarrow J^{\bullet}$ extending the identity map on $M$, and the maps $H^{r}\left(F\left(I^{\bullet}\right)\right) \rightarrow H^{r}\left(F\left(J^{\bullet}\right)\right)$ it defines are isomorphisms independent of the choice of $\alpha^{\bullet}$.

nodes.name: right derived functors R^r F
nodes.statement:
Now, for each object $M$ of C, we choose an injective resolution $M \rightarrow I^{\bullet}$, and we define

$$
\left(R^{r} F\right)(M)=H^{r}\left(F\left(I^{\bullet}\right)\right) .
$$

A morphism $\alpha: M \rightarrow N$ gives rise to a well-defined morphism $\left(R^{r} F\right)(M) \rightarrow\left(R^{r} F\right)(N)$, and these maps make $R^{r} F$ into a functor. They are called the right derived functors of $F$.

nodes.name: Lemma A.9 (maps extend to injective resolutions)
nodes.statement:
Lemma A. 9 Let $M \rightarrow I^{\bullet}$ and $N \rightarrow J^{\bullet}$ be resolutions of objects $M$ and $N$ of C. If $N \rightarrow J^{\bullet}$ is an injective resolution, then every morphism $\alpha: M \rightarrow N$ extends to a morphism\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-38_169_228_1051_918}\\
of complexes.
conclusions: every morphism $\alpha: M \rightarrow N$ extends to a morphism

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.9 (reference)
nodes.statement: Proof. Bucur and Deleanu 1968, 7.5. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Reference to Bucur and Deleanu.

nodes.name: homotopic morphisms of complexes
nodes.statement:
Two morphisms $\alpha^{\bullet}, \beta^{\bullet}: I^{\bullet} \rightarrow J^{\bullet}$ of complexes are said to be homotopic if there exists a family of morphisms $k^{r}: I^{r} \rightarrow J^{r-1}$ (a homotopy) such that

$$
\alpha^{r}-\beta^{r}=d^{r-1} \circ k^{r}+k^{r+1} \circ d^{r}
$$

for all $r$.

nodes.name: Argument that homotopic maps agree on cohomology
nodes.statement:
Note that, for every $x \in Z^{r}\left(I^{\bullet}\right) \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \operatorname{Ker}\left(d^{r}\right)$,

$$
\alpha^{r}(x)-\beta^{r}(x)=d^{r-1}\left(k^{r}(x)\right) \in \operatorname{Im}\left(d^{r-1}\right) \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} B^{r}\left(J^{\bullet}\right) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: On cycles, alpha - beta = d k is a boundary.

nodes.name: homotopic morphisms induce the same map on cohomology
nodes.statement: Therefore $\alpha^{r}(x)$ and $\beta^{r}(x)$ have the same image in $H^{r}\left(J^{\bullet}\right)$, and so homotopic morphisms define the same morphism on cohomology.
conclusions: homotopic morphisms define the same morphism on cohomology

nodes.name: Lemma A.10 (extensions are homotopic)
nodes.statement: Lemma A. 10 Let $M \rightarrow I^{\bullet}$ be a resolution of $M$, and let $N \rightarrow J^{\bullet}$ be an injective resolution $N$. Any two extensions $\alpha^{\bullet}$ and $\beta^{\bullet}$ of morphisms $M \rightarrow N$ to $I^{\bullet} \rightarrow J^{\bullet}$ are homotopic.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.10 (reference)
nodes.statement: Proof. Bucur and Deleanu 1968, 7.5. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Reference to Bucur and Deleanu.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.8
nodes.statement: This implies the second statement of Proposition A.8, because the family $\left(F\left(k^{r}\right)\right)$ is a homotopy from $F\left(\alpha^{\bullet}\right)$ to $F\left(\beta^{\bullet}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas A.9 and A.10: extensions exist and are homotopic, and F preserves homotopies.

nodes.name: Proposition A.11 (long exact sequence of derived functors)
nodes.statement:
Proposition A. 11 A short exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow 0
$$

in C gives rise to a long exact sequence

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 0 \rightarrow F(A) \rightarrow F(B) \rightarrow F(C) \rightarrow R^{1} F(A) \rightarrow \cdots \\
& \quad \cdots \rightarrow R^{r} F(A) \rightarrow R^{r} F(B) \rightarrow R^{r} F(C) \rightarrow \cdots
\end{aligned}
$$

and the association of the long exact sequence to the short exact sequence is functorial.
nodes.statement_short: A short exact sequence gives a functorial long exact sequence of right derived functors.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.11 (reference)
nodes.statement: For the proof of the proposition, see Bucur and Deleanu 1968, 7.6.
nodes.statement_short: Reference to Bucur and Deleanu.

nodes.name: Remark A.12 (characterization of derived functors)
nodes.statement_short: Derived functors are characterized by R^0F = F, vanishing on injectives, and the long exact sequence.

nodes.name: Ext via injective resolutions
nodes.statement:
Let $A \in \mathrm{C}$. If C has enough injectives, then we can define the right derived functors of the left exact functor $\operatorname{Hom}(A, \cdot)$. Denote the $r$ th right derived functor by $\operatorname{Ext}^{r}(A, \cdot)$. To compute $\operatorname{Ext}^{r}(A, B)$, we choose an injective resolution $B \rightarrow I^{\bullet}$ of $B$, and set

$$
\operatorname{Ext}^{r}(A, B)=H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}\left(A, I^{\bullet}\right)\right) .
$$

nodes.name: Ext via projective resolutions
nodes.statement:
Let $B \in \mathrm{C}$. If C has enough projectives, then we can define the right derived functors of the left exact contravariant functor $\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot, B)$. Denote the $r$ th right derived functor by $\operatorname{Ext}^{r}(\cdot, B)$. To compute $\operatorname{Ext}^{r}(A, B)$, we choose a projective resolution $P_{\bullet} \rightarrow A$ of $A$, and we set

$$
\operatorname{Ext}^{r}(A, B)=H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B\right)\right) .
$$

nodes.name: Proposition A.13 (balance of Ext)
nodes.statement: Proposition A. 13 If C has enough injectives and enough projectives, then the two definitions of $\operatorname{Ext}^{r}(A, B)$ coincide.
assumptions: C has enough injectives and enough projectives
conclusions: the two definitions of $\operatorname{Ext}^{r}(A, B)$ coincide

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition A.13
nodes.statement:
Proof. We define the $\operatorname{Ext}^{r}$ using projectives, and prove that they have the properties characterizing the right derived functors of $\operatorname{Hom}(A, \cdot)$.

First, certainly $\operatorname{Ext}^{0}(A, B)=\operatorname{Hom}(A, B)$.\\
To say that $I$ is injective means that $\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot, I)$ is exact. Therefore $\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, I\right)$ is exact, and so

$$
\operatorname{Ext}^{r}(A, I) \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, I\right)\right)=0 .
$$

Finally, if

$$
0 \rightarrow B^{\prime} \rightarrow B \rightarrow B^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow 0
$$

is exact, then because $P_{\bullet} \rightarrow A$ is a resolution of $A$ by projectives, the sequence of complexes

$$
0 \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B^{\prime \prime}\right) \rightarrow 0
$$

is exact. By a standard procedure, we get out of this a long exact sequence

$$
\cdots \rightarrow H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B^{\prime}\right)\right) \rightarrow H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B\right)\right) \rightarrow H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B^{\prime \prime}\right)\right) \rightarrow \cdots .
$$ \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Projective-defined Ext satisfies the three characterizing properties of the right derived functors of Hom(A,-).

nodes.name: strategy
nodes.statement: We define the $\operatorname{Ext}^{r}$ using projectives, and prove that they have the properties characterizing the right derived functors of $\operatorname{Hom}(A, \cdot)$.
nodes.statement_short: Check the characterizing properties

nodes.name: degree 0
nodes.statement: First, certainly $\operatorname{Ext}^{0}(A, B)=\operatorname{Hom}(A, B)$.
nodes.statement_short: Ext^0 = Hom

nodes.name: vanishing on injectives
nodes.statement:
To say that $I$ is injective means that $\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot, I)$ is exact. Therefore $\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, I\right)$ is exact, and so

$$
\operatorname{Ext}^{r}(A, I) \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, I\right)\right)=0 .
$$
nodes.statement_short: Ext^r(A, I) = 0 for injective I

nodes.name: long exact sequence
nodes.statement:
Finally, if

$$
0 \rightarrow B^{\prime} \rightarrow B \rightarrow B^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow 0
$$

is exact, then because $P_{\bullet} \rightarrow A$ is a resolution of $A$ by projectives, the sequence of complexes

$$
0 \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B^{\prime}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B^{\prime \prime}\right) \rightarrow 0
$$

is exact. By a standard procedure, we get out of this a long exact sequence

$$
\cdots \rightarrow H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B^{\prime}\right)\right) \rightarrow H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B\right)\right) \rightarrow H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}\left(P_{\bullet}, B^{\prime \prime}\right)\right) \rightarrow \cdots .
$$
nodes.statement_short: Long exact sequence from Hom(P, -)

nodes.name: Example A.14 (group cohomology as Ext)
nodes.statement_short: H^r(G,M) = Ext_G^r(Z, M), computable from any projective resolution of Z (25).

nodes.statement: H^{r}(G, M)=H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Hom}_{G}\left(P_{\bullet}, M\right)\right) . \tag{25}

nodes.name: Remark A.15 (alternative definition)
nodes.statement: Remark A. 15 It would shorten the exposition in this chapter a little by adopting the formula (25) as the definition of $H^{r}(G, M)$. This is the approach taken by Atiyah and Wall (1967), but it is not the natural definition.

nodes.name: H^2(L/K)
nodes.statement:
For a Galois extension of fields $L / K$ (possibly infinite), set

$$
H^{2}(L / K)=H^{2}\left(\operatorname{Gal}(L / K), L^{\times}\right) .
$$

nodes.name: Proposition III.1.1 (units of unramified extensions are cohomologically trivial)
nodes.statement:
Proposition 1.1 Let $L / K$ be a finite unramified extension with Galois group $G$, and let $U_{L}$ be the group of units in $L$. Then

$$
H_{T}^{r}\left(G, U_{L}\right)=0, \quad \text { all } r .
$$
assumptions: $L / K$ be a finite unramified extension with Galois group $G$
$U_{L}$ be the group of units in $L$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition III.1.1
nodes.statement_short: L^x = U_L x Z as G-modules; Hilbert 90 gives H^1(U_L) = 0; periodicity reduces to H_T^0, i.e., surjectivity of the norm on units.

nodes.name: decomposition
nodes.statement_short: L^x = U_L . pi^Z (26)

nodes.statement: L^{\times}=U_{L} \cdot \pi^{\mathbb{Z}} \simeq U_{L} \times \mathbb{Z} . \tag{26}

nodes.name: G-module decomposition
nodes.statement:
Since $L$ is unramified over $K$, we can choose $\pi \in K$. Then $\tau \alpha=\tau\left(u \pi^{m}\right)=(\tau u) \pi^{m}$ for $\tau \in \operatorname{Gal}(L / K)$, and so (26) becomes a decomposition of $G$-modules when we let\\
$G$ act trivially on $\pi^{\mathbb{Z}} \simeq \mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: With pi in K, (26) is a decomposition of G-modules

nodes.name: Hilbert 90
nodes.statement: Therefore, $H^{r}\left(G, U_{L}\right)$ is a direct summand of $H^{r}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)$ (see II, 1.25). Since $H^{1}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)=0$ by Hilbert's theorem 90 (II, 1.22), this shows that $H^{1}\left(G, U_{L}\right)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct summand of H^r(L^x); Hilbert 90 gives H^1 = 0

nodes.name: reduce to H^0
nodes.statement: Because $G$ is cyclic, to complete the proof of the theorem, it suffices (by II, 3.4) to show that $H_{T}^{0}\left(G, U_{L}\right)=0$. This is accomplished by the next proposition.
nodes.statement_short: By periodicity it suffices to show H_T^0 = 0

nodes.name: Proposition III.1.2 (norm surjective on units, unramified)
nodes.statement: Proposition 1.2 Let $L / K$ be a finite unramified extension. Then the norm map $\operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}: U_{L} \rightarrow$ $U_{K}$ is surjective.
assumptions: $L / K$ be a finite unramified extension

nodes.name: residue fields l, k
nodes.statement: Let $l$ and $k$ be the residue fields of $L$ and $K$.

nodes.name: G = Gal(l/k) for unramified L/K
nodes.statement: Because $L / K$ is unramified, the action of $G$ on $\mathcal{O}_{L}$ defines an isomorphism $G \simeq \operatorname{Gal}(l / k)$.

nodes.name: Lemma III.1.3 (graded pieces of the unit filtration)
nodes.statement:
Lemma 1.3 For $m>0$, let $U_{L}^{(m)}=1+\mathfrak{m}_{L}^{m}$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
U_{L} / U_{L}^{(1)} & \xrightarrow{\simeq} l^{\times} \\
U_{L}^{(m)} / U_{L}^{(m+1)} & \approx l
\end{aligned}
$$

as $G$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: U_L/U_L^(1) = l^x and U_L^(m)/U_L^(m+1) = l as G-modules.

nodes.name: higher unit groups U_L^(m)
nodes.statement: For $m>0$, let $U_{L}^{(m)}=1+\mathfrak{m}_{L}^{m}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.1.3
nodes.statement:
Proof. Let $\pi$ be a prime element of $K$. It remains prime in $L$, and

$$
U_{L}^{(m)}=\left\{1+a \pi^{m} \mid a \in \mathcal{O}_{L}\right\} .
$$

The maps

$$
\begin{aligned}
u \mapsto u & \bmod \mathfrak{m}_{L}: U_{L} \rightarrow l^{\times} \\
1+a \pi^{m} \mapsto a & \bmod \mathfrak{m}_{L}: U_{L}^{(m)} \rightarrow l
\end{aligned}
$$

induce the required isomorphisms. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Reduce u mod m_L and 1 + a pi^m -> a mod m_L.

nodes.name: prime element
nodes.statement:
Let $\pi$ be a prime element of $K$. It remains prime in $L$, and

$$
U_{L}^{(m)}=\left\{1+a \pi^{m} \mid a \in \mathcal{O}_{L}\right\} .
$$
nodes.statement_short: pi in K stays prime; describe U_L^(m)

nodes.name: reduction maps
nodes.statement:
The maps

$$
\begin{aligned}
u \mapsto u & \bmod \mathfrak{m}_{L}: U_{L} \rightarrow l^{\times} \\
1+a \pi^{m} \mapsto a & \bmod \mathfrak{m}_{L}: U_{L}^{(m)} \rightarrow l
\end{aligned}
$$

induce the required isomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: Reduction maps give the isomorphisms

nodes.name: Lemma III.1.4 (residue field multiplicative group)
nodes.statement: Lemma 1.4 For all $r, H_{T}^{r}\left(G, l^{\times}\right)=0$. In particular, the norm map $l^{\times} \rightarrow k^{\times}$is surjective.
conclusions: In particular, the norm map $l^{\times} \rightarrow k^{\times}$is surjective.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.1.4
nodes.statement: Proof. By Hilbert's Theorem 90 (II, 1.22), $H^{1}\left(G, l^{\times}\right)=0$, and because $l^{\times}$is finite, its Herbrand quotient $h\left(l^{\times}\right)=1$ (see II 3.8). Therefore $H^{2}\left(G, l^{\times}\right)=0$, and this implies that all the groups are zero (by II, 3.4). \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Hilbert 90 plus Herbrand quotient 1 for finite modules, then periodicity.

nodes.name: Lemma III.1.5 (residue field additive group)
nodes.statement: Lemma 1.5 The group $H_{T}^{r}(G, l)=0$ for all $r$. In particular, the trace map $l \rightarrow k$ is surjective.
conclusions: In particular, the trace map $l \rightarrow k$ is surjective.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.1.5
nodes.statement: Proof. In (II, 1.24) this is proved for $r>0$, which implies it for all $r$ (by II, 3.4). \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Additive Hilbert 90 plus periodicity.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition III.1.2
nodes.statement:
Proof (of Proposition 1.2) There are commutative diagrams $(m>0)$\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-42_215_621_2038_726}\\
Consider $u \in U_{K}$. Because the norm map $l^{\times} \rightarrow k^{\times}$is surjective, there exists a $v_{0} \in$ $U_{L}$ such that $\operatorname{Nm}\left(v_{0}\right)$ and $u$ have the same image in $k^{\times}$, i.e., such that $u / \operatorname{Nm}\left(v_{0}\right) \in$ $U_{K}^{(1)}$. Because the trace map $l \rightarrow k$ is surjective, there exists a $v_{1} \in U_{L}^{(1)}$ such that $\operatorname{Nm}\left(v_{1}\right) \equiv u / \operatorname{Nm}\left(v_{0}\right) \bmod U_{K}^{(2)}$. Continuing in this fashion, we obtain a sequence of elements $v_{0}, v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}, \ldots, v_{i} \in U_{L}^{(i)}$, such that $u / \operatorname{Nm}\left(v_{0} \cdots v_{i}\right) \in U_{K}^{(i+1)}$. Let $v=$ $\lim _{m \rightarrow \infty} \prod_{j=0}^{m} v_{j}$. Then $u / \operatorname{Nm}(v) \in \bigcap U_{K}^{(i)}=\{1\}$. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Successive approximation: lift through the unit filtration using surjectivity of norm and trace on residue fields, then take the limit.

nodes.name: first approximation
nodes.statement:
There are commutative diagrams $(m>0)$\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-42_215_621_2038_726}\\
Consider $u \in U_{K}$. Because the norm map $l^{\times} \rightarrow k^{\times}$is surjective, there exists a $v_{0} \in$ $U_{L}$ such that $\operatorname{Nm}\left(v_{0}\right)$ and $u$ have the same image in $k^{\times}$, i.e., such that $u / \operatorname{Nm}\left(v_{0}\right) \in$ $U_{K}^{(1)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Use surjectivity of l^x -> k^x to find v_0

nodes.name: next approximation
nodes.statement: Because the trace map $l \rightarrow k$ is surjective, there exists a $v_{1} \in U_{L}^{(1)}$ such that $\operatorname{Nm}\left(v_{1}\right) \equiv u / \operatorname{Nm}\left(v_{0}\right) \bmod U_{K}^{(2)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Use surjectivity of the trace to find v_1

nodes.name: continue
nodes.statement: Continuing in this fashion, we obtain a sequence of elements $v_{0}, v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}, \ldots, v_{i} \in U_{L}^{(i)}$, such that $u / \operatorname{Nm}\left(v_{0} \cdots v_{i}\right) \in U_{K}^{(i+1)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate to get v_i

nodes.name: limit
nodes.statement: Let $v=$ $\lim _{m \rightarrow \infty} \prod_{j=0}^{m} v_{j}$. Then $u / \operatorname{Nm}(v) \in \bigcap U_{K}^{(i)}=\{1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: The limit v has norm u

nodes.name: Corollary III.1.6 (infinite unramified extensions)
nodes.statement: Corollary 1.6 Let $L / K$ be an infinite unramified extension with Galois group $G$. Then $H^{r}\left(G, U_{L}\right)=0$ for $r>0$ (continuous cochains).
assumptions: $L / K$ be an infinite unramified extension with Galois group $G$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary III.1.6
nodes.statement:
Proof. The field $L$ is a union of finite extensions $K^{\prime}$ of $K$, and so (see II, 4.2),

$$
H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Gal}(L / K), U_{L}\right) \simeq \lim _{\longrightarrow K^{\prime}} H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\prime} / K\right), U_{K^{\prime}}\right)=0 .
$$ \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Direct limit over finite subextensions (II, 4.2).

nodes.name: H^2(G,L^x) = H^2(G,Z) via ord, unramified
nodes.statement:
As $H^{2}\left(G, U_{L}\right)=0=H^{3}\left(G, U_{L}\right)$, the cohomology sequence of the short exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow U_{L} \rightarrow L^{\times} \xrightarrow{\operatorname{ord}_{L}} \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0,
$$

gives an isomorphism

$$
H^{2}\left(G, L^{\times}\right) \xrightarrow[\simeq]{H^{2}\left(\operatorname{ord}_{L}\right)} H^{2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) .
$$

nodes.name: H^1(G,Q/Z) = H^2(G,Z)
nodes.statement:
The groups $H^{r}(G, \mathbb{Q})$ are torsion for $r>0$ (see II, 4.3) and uniquely divisible (because $\mathbb{Q}$ is), and hence zero. Therefore the cohomology sequence of the short exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0
$$

(trivial $G$-actions) gives an isomorphism

$$
H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{\delta} H^{2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) .
$$

nodes.name: invariant map inv_{L/K} (unramified)
nodes.statement:
The composite of

$$
H^{2}(L / K) \xrightarrow[\simeq]{\text { ord }_{L}} H^{2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \stackrel{\delta}{\simeq} H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\text {cts }}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{f \mapsto f(\sigma)} \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}
$$

is called the invariant map

$$
\operatorname{inv}_{L / K}: H^{2}(L / K) \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z} .
$$
nodes.statement_short: inv_{L/K}: H^2(L/K) -> H^2(G,Z) -> H^1(G,Q/Z) = Hom(G,Q/Z) -> Q/Z, the last map evaluating at Frobenius.

nodes.name: invariant maps compatible with inflation
nodes.statement:
Consider a tower of field extensions

$$
E \supset L \supset K
$$

with both $E$ and $L$ unramified (hence Galois) over $K$. Then\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-43_204_374_2307_848}\\
commutes, because all the maps in the definition of inv are compatible with Inf.

nodes.name: Theorem III.1.7 (invariant map for K^un)
nodes.statement:
Theorem 1.7 There exists a unique isomorphism

$$
\operatorname{inv}_{K}: H^{2}\left(K^{\text {un }} / K\right) \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z},
$$

with the property that, for every $L \subset K^{\text {un }}$ of finite degree $n$ over $K, \operatorname{inv}_{K}$ induces the isomorphism

$$
\operatorname{inv}_{L / K}: H^{2}(L / K) \rightarrow \frac{1}{[L: K]} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z} .
$$
nodes.statement_short: inv_K: H^2(K^un/K) = Q/Z restricting to H^2(L/K) = (1/[L:K])Z/Z for finite unramified L.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem III.1.7
nodes.statement: Proof. This is an immediate consequence of the above discussion. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the invariant maps and their compatibility with inflation.

nodes.name: Proposition III.1.8 (restriction multiplies invariants by the degree)
nodes.statement: Proposition 1.8 Let $L$ be a finite extension of $K$ of degree $n$, and let $K^{\text {un }}$ and $L^{\text {un }}$ be the largest unramified extensions of $K$ and $L$. Then the following diagram commutes:
nodes.statement_short: For L/K of degree n, Res: H^2(K^un/K) -> H^2(L^un/L) corresponds to multiplication by n on Q/Z (diagram (27)).

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition III.1.8
nodes.statement:
Proof. The largest unramified extension of a local field is obtained by adjoining all $m$ th roots of 1 for $m$ not divisible by the residue characteristic. Therefore, $L^{\text {un }}=L \cdot K^{\text {un }}$, and so the map

$$
\tau \mapsto \tau \mid K^{\text {un }}: \operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\text {un }} / L\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\text {un }} / K\right)
$$

is injective. The map denoted Res in (27) is that defined by the compatible homomorphisms

$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
\operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\text {un }} / K\right) & \leftarrow & \operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\text {un }} / L\right) \\
K^{\text {un× }} & \rightarrow & L^{\text {un× }}
\end{array}
$$

(II, 1.27b).\\
Let $\Gamma_{K}=\operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\text {un }} / K\right)$ and $\Gamma_{L}=\operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\text {un }} / L\right)$, and consider the diagram,\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-44_242_1206_1636_432}

Here $e$ is the ramification index for $L / K$ and $f$ is the residue class degree. The first square is obtained from the commutative square\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-44_180_262_2029_905}\\
The second square expresses the fact that the restriction map commutes with the boundary map. Apart from the factor " $e$ ", the third square is\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-44_231_512_2365_776}

The Frobenius elements $\sigma_{K}$ and $\sigma_{L}$ are determined by the fact that they induce $x \mapsto x^{q}$ and $x \mapsto x^{q^{f}}$ respectively on the residue fields, where $q=|k|$ and $q^{f}=|l|$, and so $\sigma_{L} \mid K^{\text {un }}=\sigma_{K}^{f}$. It is now clear that the square commutes, and since $n=e f$, this proves the proposition. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Factor the invariant map into three squares: ord_L = e ord_K, Res commutes with delta, and Frobenius restricts as sigma_K^f; then n = ef.

nodes.name: L^un = L K^un
nodes.statement:
The largest unramified extension of a local field is obtained by adjoining all $m$ th roots of 1 for $m$ not divisible by the residue characteristic. Therefore, $L^{\text {un }}=L \cdot K^{\text {un }}$, and so the map

$$
\tau \mapsto \tau \mid K^{\text {un }}: \operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\text {un }} / L\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\text {un }} / K\right)
$$

is injective.
nodes.statement_short: L^un = L K^un, so Gal(L^un/L) injects into Gal(K^un/K)

nodes.name: the map Res
nodes.statement_short: Res is defined by compatible homomorphisms

nodes.name: big diagram
nodes.statement:
Let $\Gamma_{K}=\operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\text {un }} / K\right)$ and $\Gamma_{L}=\operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\text {un }} / L\right)$, and consider the diagram,\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-44_242_1206_1636_432}

Here $e$ is the ramification index for $L / K$ and $f$ is the residue class degree. The first square is obtained from the commutative square\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-44_180_262_2029_905}\\
The second square expresses the fact that the restriction map commutes with the boundary map.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose into three squares with e and f

nodes.name: third square
nodes.statement_short: sigma_L restricts to sigma_K^f; n = ef

nodes.name: local fundamental class u_{L/K} (unramified)
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a finite unramified extension of $K$ with Galois group $G$, and let $n=[L: K]$. The local fundamental class $u_{L / K}$ is the element of $H^{2}(L / K)$ mapped to the generator $\frac{1}{[L: K]}$ of $\frac{1}{[L: K]} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z}$ by the invariant map $\operatorname{inv}_{L / K}: H^{2}(L / K) \xrightarrow{\simeq} \frac{1}{[L: K]} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: Tate's theorem applies to unramified L/K
nodes.statement:
The pair $\left(G, L^{\times}\right)$satisfies the hypotheses of Tate's theorem (II, 3.11), ${ }^{1}$ and so cup-product with the fundamental class $u_{L / K}$ defines an isomorphism

$$
H_{T}^{r}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H_{T}^{r+2}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)
$$

for all $r \in \mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: Computation of a cocycle for the fundamental class
nodes.statement:
