A prime element $\pi$ of $K$ is also a prime element of $L$, and defines a decomposition

$$
L^{\times}=U_{L} \cdot \pi^{\mathbb{Z}} \simeq U_{L} \times \mathbb{Z}
$$

of $G$-modules. Thus

$$
H^{r}\left(G, L^{\times}\right) \simeq H^{r}\left(G, U_{L}\right) \oplus H^{r}\left(G, \pi^{\mathbb{Z}}\right) .
$$

Choose a generator $\sigma$ of $G$ (e.g., the Frobenius generator), and let

$$
f \in H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})
$$

be the element such that $f\left(\sigma^{i}\right)=\frac{i}{n} \bmod \mathbb{Z}$ for all $i$. It generates $H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})$.\\
From the exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0
$$

and the fact that $H^{r}(G, \mathbb{Q})=0$ for all $r$, we obtain an isomorphism

$$
\delta: H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H^{2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) .
$$

According to the description of $\delta$ in (II, 1.21), to construct $\delta f$, we first choose a lifting of $f$ to 1 -cochain $\tilde{f}: G \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$. We take $\tilde{f}$ to be the map $\sigma^{i} \mapsto \frac{i}{n}$, where $0 \leq i<n-1$. Then

$$
d \tilde{f}\left(\sigma^{i}, \sigma^{j}\right)=\sigma^{i} \tilde{f}\left(\sigma^{j}\right)-\tilde{f}\left(\sigma^{i+j}\right)+\tilde{f}\left(\sigma^{i}\right)=\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
0 & \text { if } & i+j \leq n-1 \\
1 & \text { if } & i+j>n-1 .
\end{array}\right.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Lift the generator f of H^1(G,Q/Z) to Q and compute its coboundary, which is 0 or 1 according as i+j < n.

nodes.name: decomposition
nodes.statement:
A prime element $\pi$ of $K$ is also a prime element of $L$, and defines a decomposition

$$
L^{\times}=U_{L} \cdot \pi^{\mathbb{Z}} \simeq U_{L} \times \mathbb{Z}
$$

of $G$-modules. Thus

$$
H^{r}\left(G, L^{\times}\right) \simeq H^{r}\left(G, U_{L}\right) \oplus H^{r}\left(G, \pi^{\mathbb{Z}}\right) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: pi gives L^x = U_L x Z

nodes.name: generator f
nodes.statement:
Choose a generator $\sigma$ of $G$ (e.g., the Frobenius generator), and let

$$
f \in H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})
$$

be the element such that $f\left(\sigma^{i}\right)=\frac{i}{n} \bmod \mathbb{Z}$ for all $i$. It generates $H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})$.
nodes.statement_short: f(sigma^i) = i/n generates H^1(G, Q/Z)

nodes.name: delta iso
nodes.statement:
From the exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0
$$

and the fact that $H^{r}(G, \mathbb{Q})=0$ for all $r$, we obtain an isomorphism

$$
\delta: H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H^{2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: delta: H^1(G,Q/Z) = H^2(G,Z)

nodes.name: compute d f~
nodes.statement:
According to the description of $\delta$ in (II, 1.21), to construct $\delta f$, we first choose a lifting of $f$ to 1 -cochain $\tilde{f}: G \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$. We take $\tilde{f}$ to be the map $\sigma^{i} \mapsto \frac{i}{n}$, where $0 \leq i<n-1$. Then

$$
d \tilde{f}\left(\sigma^{i}, \sigma^{j}\right)=\sigma^{i} \tilde{f}\left(\sigma^{j}\right)-\tilde{f}\left(\sigma^{i+j}\right)+\tilde{f}\left(\sigma^{i}\right)=\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
0 & \text { if } & i+j \leq n-1 \\
1 & \text { if } & i+j>n-1 .
\end{array}\right.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Coboundary of the lift is 0 or 1

nodes.name: cocycle representing the unramified fundamental class
nodes.statement:
When we identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with the subgroup $\pi^{\mathbb{Z}}$ of $L^{\times}$, we find that the fundamental class $u_{L / K} \in H^{2}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)$is represented by the cocycle:

$$
\varphi\left(\sigma^{i}, \sigma^{j}\right)=\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
1 & \text { if } & i+j \leq n-1 \\
\pi & \text { if } & i+j>n-1
\end{array}\right.
$$
conclusions: the fundamental class $u_{L / K} \in H^{2}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)$is represented by the cocycle

nodes.name: boundary maps used for the Artin map
nodes.statement:
From the exact sequences

$$
\begin{gathered}
0 \rightarrow I \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}[G] \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0 \\
0 \rightarrow L^{\times} \rightarrow L^{\times}(\varphi) \rightarrow I \rightarrow 0
\end{gathered}
$$

(see the proof of II, 3.11) we obtain boundary maps

$$
\begin{aligned}
& H^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H^{-1}(G, I) \\
& H^{-1}(G, I) \rightarrow H^{0}\left(G, L^{\times}\right),
\end{aligned}
$$

which are isomorphisms because $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ and $L^{\times}(\varphi)$ have trivial cohomology. Here $L^{\times}(\varphi)$ is the splitting module $L^{\times} \oplus \bigoplus_{\sigma \in G, \sigma \neq 1} \mathbb{Z} x_{\sigma}$ of $\varphi$.

Finally, $H^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} H_{1}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \simeq G$ (see II, 2.7).
nodes.statement_short: The splitting module L^x(phi) and augmentation sequence give isomorphisms H^{-2}(G,Z) -> H^{-1}(G,I) -> H^0(G,L^x).

nodes.name: Proposition III.1.9 (Frobenius maps to the class of pi)
nodes.statement_short: For unramified L/K, the Tate isomorphism G -> K^x / Nm L^x sends Frobenius to the class of a prime element pi.

nodes.name: independence of the prime element
nodes.statement: Note that, because all units in $K$ are norms from $L^{\times}$(see 1.2), the class of $\pi \bmod$ $\operatorname{Nm}\left(L^{\times}\right)$is independent of the prime element $\pi$. On the other hand, the $G$-module $L^{\times}(\varphi)$ and the map depend on the choice of the generator $\sigma$ for $G$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition III.1.9
nodes.statement:
Proof. From the construction of the isomorphism $H^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \simeq G$, we see that the image of $\sigma$ under the boundary map $H^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H^{-1}\left(G, I_{G}\right) \subset I_{G} / I_{G}^{2}$ is represented by $\sigma-1$.

The boundary map $H^{-1}\left(G, I_{G}\right) \rightarrow H^{0}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)$is that given by the snake lemma from the diagram (we write $I$ for $I_{G}$ ):\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-46_464_1042_2090_511}

The vertical maps connecting the rows are $\mathrm{Nm}_{G}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \sigma^{i}$. The element $(\sigma-1)+I^{2}$ is the image of $x_{\sigma}+I \cdot L^{\times}(\varphi)$ in $L^{\times}(\varphi)_{G}$, and $\operatorname{Nm}_{G}\left(x_{\sigma}+I \cdot L^{\times}(\varphi)\right)$ is the sum of the elements:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{\sigma} & =x_{\sigma} \\
\sigma x_{\sigma} & =x_{\sigma^{2}}-x_{\sigma}+\varphi(\sigma, \sigma) \\
\sigma^{2} x_{\sigma} & =x_{\sigma^{3}}-x_{\sigma^{2}}+\varphi\left(\sigma, \sigma^{2}\right) \\
\cdots & \cdots \\
\sigma^{n-1} x_{\sigma} & ={ }^{\prime} x_{1},-x_{\sigma^{n-1}}+\varphi\left(\sigma, \sigma^{n-1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

On summing these, remembering that ' $x_{1}$ ' $=\varphi(1,1)=1$ and that + on the factor $L^{\times}$of $L(\varphi)$ is actually •, we find that

$$
\operatorname{Nm}_{G}\left(x_{\sigma}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \varphi\left(\sigma, \sigma^{i}\right)=\pi .
$$

This completes the proof. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Chase sigma through the two boundary maps via the snake lemma; the norm of x_sigma is the product of cocycle values, which equals pi.

nodes.name: first boundary
nodes.statement: From the construction of the isomorphism $H^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \simeq G$, we see that the image of $\sigma$ under the boundary map $H^{-2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H^{-1}\left(G, I_{G}\right) \subset I_{G} / I_{G}^{2}$ is represented by $\sigma-1$.
nodes.statement_short: sigma maps to sigma - 1 in I/I^2

nodes.name: snake lemma
nodes.statement:
The boundary map $H^{-1}\left(G, I_{G}\right) \rightarrow H^{0}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)$is that given by the snake lemma from the diagram (we write $I$ for $I_{G}$ ):\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-46_464_1042_2090_511}
nodes.statement_short: Second boundary via the snake lemma

nodes.name: norm of x_sigma
nodes.statement:
The vertical maps connecting the rows are $\mathrm{Nm}_{G}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \sigma^{i}$. The element $(\sigma-1)+I^{2}$ is the image of $x_{\sigma}+I \cdot L^{\times}(\varphi)$ in $L^{\times}(\varphi)_{G}$, and $\operatorname{Nm}_{G}\left(x_{\sigma}+I \cdot L^{\times}(\varphi)\right)$ is the sum of the elements:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{\sigma} & =x_{\sigma} \\
\sigma x_{\sigma} & =x_{\sigma^{2}}-x_{\sigma}+\varphi(\sigma, \sigma) \\
\sigma^{2} x_{\sigma} & =x_{\sigma^{3}}-x_{\sigma^{2}}+\varphi\left(\sigma, \sigma^{2}\right) \\
\cdots & \cdots \\
\sigma^{n-1} x_{\sigma} & ={ }^{\prime} x_{1},-x_{\sigma^{n-1}}+\varphi\left(\sigma, \sigma^{n-1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
nodes.statement_short: Expand Nm_G(x_sigma) termwise

nodes.name: sum
nodes.statement:
On summing these, remembering that ' $x_{1}$ ' $=\varphi(1,1)=1$ and that + on the factor $L^{\times}$of $L(\varphi)$ is actually •, we find that

$$
\operatorname{Nm}_{G}\left(x_{\sigma}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \varphi\left(\sigma, \sigma^{i}\right)=\pi .
$$

This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: The product of cocycle values is pi

nodes.name: Remark III.1.10
nodes.statement: Remark 1.10 The above proof of Proposition 1.9, using Tate's original definition of the isomorphism $H^{r}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H^{r+2}(G, C)$, is simpler than that found in other references, which uses the description of the map in terms of cup products.

nodes.name: inflation-restriction for H^2 of towers
nodes.statement:
Because of Hilbert's Theorem 90 (II, 1.22), there is an exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow H^{2}(L / K) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{Inf}} H^{2}(E / K) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{Res}} H^{2}(E / L)
$$

for any tower of Galois extensions $E \supset L \supset K$ (see II, 1.36).

nodes.name: Theorem III.2.1 (invariant map for local fields)
nodes.statement:
Theorem 2.1 For every local field $K$, there exists a canonical isomorphism

$$
\operatorname{inv}_{K}: H^{2}\left(K^{\mathrm{al}} / K\right) \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z} .
$$

Let $L$ be a Galois extension of $K$ of degree $n<\infty$. Then the diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-47_204_945_1961_557}

(28)\\
commutes, and therefore defines an isomorphism

$$
\operatorname{inv}_{L / K}: H^{2}(L / K) \rightarrow \frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z} .
$$
nodes.statement_short: inv_K: H^2(K^al/K) = Q/Z, compatible with restriction (times n), inducing H^2(L/K) = (1/n)Z/Z for L/K Galois of degree n.

nodes.name: Lemma III.2.2 (H^2(L/K) contains (1/n)Z/Z)
nodes.statement: Lemma 2.2 If $L / K$ is Galois of finite degree $n$, then $H^{2}(L / K)$ contains a subgroup canonically isomorphic to $\frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z}$.
assumptions: $L / K$ is Galois of finite degree $n$
conclusions: $H^{2}(L / K)$ contains a subgroup canonically isomorphic to $\frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z}$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.2.2
nodes.statement:
Proof. Consider the diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-48_198_953_427_556}\\
Since the two inflation maps are injective, so also is the first vertical map, but 1.8 shows that the kernel of the restriction map on the top row is canonically isomorphic to $\frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z}$. □
nodes.statement_short: Inflation is injective; Proposition 1.8 identifies the kernel of restriction on the unramified level with (1/n)Z/Z.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem III.2.1, reduction
nodes.statement: To complete the proof of Theorem 2.1, it suffices to prove that the map $\frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow$ $H^{2}(L / K)$ is an isomorphism. There are two different approaches to proving this. In the next chapter on Brauer groups, we shall show that $H^{2}\left(K^{\text {un }} / K\right) \simeq H^{2}\left(K^{\text {al }} / K\right)$ (every central simple algebra over $K$ is split by an unramified extension; see IV §4), and so the vertical maps in the above diagram are isomorphisms. The second proof, which we now present, shows that $\left|H^{2}(L / K)\right| \leq n$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing the embedding (1/n)Z/Z -> H^2(L/K) is onto, i.e. |H^2(L/K)| <= n.

nodes.name: Lemma III.2.3 (cohomologically trivial open lattice)
nodes.statement: Lemma 2.3 Let $L$ be a finite Galois extension of $K$ with Galois group $G$. Then there exists an open subgroup $V$ of $\mathcal{O}_{L}$, stable under $G$, such that $H^{r}(G, V)=0$ for all $r>0$.
assumptions: $L$ be a finite Galois extension of $K$ with Galois group $G$
conclusions: there exists an open subgroup $V$ of $\mathcal{O}_{L}$, stable under $G$, such that $H^{r}(G, V)=0$ for all $r>0$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.2.3
nodes.statement:
Proof. Let $\left\{x_{\tau} \mid \tau \in G\right\}$ be a normal basis for $L$ over $K$ (see FT, 5.18). The $x_{\tau}$ have a common denominator $d$ in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ (see ANT, 2.6). After replacing each $x_{\tau}$ with $d \cdot x_{\tau}$, we may suppose that they lie in $\mathcal{O}_{L}$. Take $V=\sum \mathcal{O}_{K} x_{\tau}$. It is stable under $G$ because the normal basis is. Let $\pi$ be a prime element of $\mathcal{O}_{L}$. Then $V \supset \pi^{m} \mathcal{O}_{L}$ for some $m>0$, which shows that $V$ is open (it is union of cosets of $\pi^{m} \mathcal{O}_{L}$ ). Finally,

$$
V \simeq \mathcal{O}_{K}[G] \simeq \operatorname{Ind}^{G} \mathcal{O}_{K}
$$

as $G$-modules, and so $H^{r}(G, V)=0$ for all $r>0$ (II, 1.12). \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Take V = sum O_K x_tau for an integral normal basis; V = O_K[G] is induced, hence acyclic.

nodes.name: integral normal basis
nodes.statement: Let $\left\{x_{\tau} \mid \tau \in G\right\}$ be a normal basis for $L$ over $K$ (see FT, 5.18). The $x_{\tau}$ have a common denominator $d$ in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ (see ANT, 2.6). After replacing each $x_{\tau}$ with $d \cdot x_{\tau}$, we may suppose that they lie in $\mathcal{O}_{L}$.
nodes.statement_short: Scale a normal basis into O_L

nodes.name: define V
nodes.statement: Take $V=\sum \mathcal{O}_{K} x_{\tau}$. It is stable under $G$ because the normal basis is.
nodes.statement_short: V = sum O_K x_tau is G-stable

nodes.name: V open
nodes.statement: Let $\pi$ be a prime element of $\mathcal{O}_{L}$. Then $V \supset \pi^{m} \mathcal{O}_{L}$ for some $m>0$, which shows that $V$ is open (it is union of cosets of $\pi^{m} \mathcal{O}_{L}$ ).
nodes.statement_short: V contains pi^m O_L, so is open

nodes.name: V induced
nodes.statement:
Finally,

$$
V \simeq \mathcal{O}_{K}[G] \simeq \operatorname{Ind}^{G} \mathcal{O}_{K}
$$

as $G$-modules, and so $H^{r}(G, V)=0$ for all $r>0$ (II, 1.12).
nodes.statement_short: V = Ind^G O_K is acyclic

nodes.name: Lemma III.2.4 (cohomologically trivial open subgroup of units)
nodes.statement: Lemma 2.4 Let $L, K$, and $G$, be as in the last lemma. Then there exists an open subgroup $V$ of $U_{L}$ stable under $G$ such that $H^{r}(G, V)=0$ for all $r>0$.
assumptions: $L, K$, and $G$, be as in the last lemma
conclusions: there exists an open subgroup $V$ of $U_{L}$ stable under $G$ such that $H^{r}(G, V)=0$ for all $r>0$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.2.4
nodes.statement:
Proof. I prove this only for $K$ of characteristic zero. ${ }^{2}$ The power series

$$
e^{x}=1+x+\cdots+x^{n} / n!+\cdots
$$

converges for $\operatorname{ord}(x)>\operatorname{ord}(p) /(p-1)$ (ANT, 7.29). It defines an isomorphism of an open neighbourhood of 0 in $L$ onto an open neighbourhood of 1 in $L^{\times}$, with inverse mapping

$$
\log (x)=(x-1)-(x-1)^{2} / 2+(x-1)^{3} / 3-\cdots .
$$

Both maps commute with the actions of $G$ (because $G$ acts continuously). If $V^{\prime}$ is an open neighbourhood of 0 as in (2.3), then $\pi^{M} V^{\prime}$ will have the same properties, and we can take $V=\exp \left(\pi^{M} V^{\prime}\right)$ with $M$ chosen to be sufficiently large that the exponential function is defined and an isomorphism on $\pi^{M} V^{\prime}$. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: In characteristic 0, the exponential maps a small multiple of the lattice of Lemma 2.3 G-equivariantly onto an open subgroup of units.

nodes.name: char 0
nodes.statement: I prove this only for $K$ of characteristic zero.
nodes.statement_short: Only characteristic zero is treated

nodes.name: exponential
nodes.statement:
The power series

$$
e^{x}=1+x+\cdots+x^{n} / n!+\cdots
$$

converges for $\operatorname{ord}(x)>\operatorname{ord}(p) /(p-1)$ (ANT, 7.29). It defines an isomorphism of an open neighbourhood of 0 in $L$ onto an open neighbourhood of 1 in $L^{\times}$, with inverse mapping

$$
\log (x)=(x-1)-(x-1)^{2} / 2+(x-1)^{3} / 3-\cdots .
$$
nodes.statement_short: exp and log are inverse near 0 and 1

nodes.name: G-equivariance
nodes.statement: Both maps commute with the actions of $G$
nodes.statement_short: exp and log are G-equivariant

nodes.name: define V
nodes.statement: If $V^{\prime}$ is an open neighbourhood of 0 as in (2.3), then $\pi^{M} V^{\prime}$ will have the same properties, and we can take $V=\exp \left(\pi^{M} V^{\prime}\right)$ with $M$ chosen to be sufficiently large that the exponential function is defined and an isomorphism on $\pi^{M} V^{\prime}$.
nodes.statement_short: V = exp(pi^M V') works

nodes.name: Lemma III.2.5 (Herbrand quotients of units and L^x)
nodes.statement: Lemma 2.5 Let $L / K$ be a cyclic extension of degree $n$; then $h\left(U_{L}\right)=1$ and $h\left(L^{\times}\right)=n$.
assumptions: $L / K$ be a cyclic extension of degree $n$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.2.5
nodes.statement:
Proof. Let $V$ be an open subgroup of $U_{L}$ with $H^{r}(G, V)=0$ for all $r$. Because $U_{L}$ is compact, the quotient $U_{L} / V$ is finite, and so $h\left(U_{L}\right)=h(V)=1$ by II, 3.9. Now $h\left(L^{\times}\right)=h\left(U_{L}\right) \cdot h(\mathbb{Z})=h(\mathbb{Z})$, and

$$
h(\mathbb{Z})=\left|H_{T}^{0}(G, \mathbb{Z})\right| /\left|H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Z})\right|=\left|H_{T}^{0}(G, \mathbb{Z})\right|=|\mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}|=n .
$$ \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: h(U_L) = h(V) = 1 since U_L/V is finite; h(L^x) = h(U_L) h(Z) = n.

nodes.name: h(U_L)=1
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be an open subgroup of $U_{L}$ with $H^{r}(G, V)=0$ for all $r$. Because $U_{L}$ is compact, the quotient $U_{L} / V$ is finite, and so $h\left(U_{L}\right)=h(V)=1$ by II, 3.9.
nodes.statement_short: Finite index V gives h(U_L) = h(V) = 1

nodes.name: h(L^x)=n
nodes.statement:
Now $h\left(L^{\times}\right)=h\left(U_{L}\right) \cdot h(\mathbb{Z})=h(\mathbb{Z})$, and

$$
h(\mathbb{Z})=\left|H_{T}^{0}(G, \mathbb{Z})\right| /\left|H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Z})\right|=\left|H_{T}^{0}(G, \mathbb{Z})\right|=|\mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}|=n .
$$
nodes.statement_short: h(L^x) = h(Z) = n

nodes.name: Lemma III.2.6 (order of H^2(L/K))
nodes.statement: Lemma 2.6 Let $L$ be a finite Galois extension of $K$ of order $n$, then $H^{2}(L / K)$ has order $n$.
assumptions: $L$ be a finite Galois extension of $K$ of order $n$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.2.6
nodes.statement:
Proof. We know that the order of $H^{2}(L / K)$ is divisible by $n$, and that it equals $n$ when $L / K$ is cyclic. We prove the lemma by induction on $[L: K]$. Because the group $\operatorname{Gal}(L / K)$ is solvable (ANT, 7.59), there exists a Galois extension $K^{\prime} / K$ with $L \supsetneqq K^{\prime} \supsetneqq K$. From the exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow H^{2}\left(K^{\prime} / K\right) \rightarrow H^{2}(L / K) \rightarrow H^{2}\left(L / K^{\prime}\right)
$$

we see that

$$
\left|H^{2}(L / K)\right| \leq\left|H^{2}\left(K^{\prime} / K\right)\right| \cdot\left|H^{2}\left(L / K^{\prime}\right)\right|=n .
$$ \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Induction on [L:K] using solvability of local Galois groups and the inflation-restriction sequence; the cyclic case is known.

nodes.name: known facts
nodes.statement: We know that the order of $H^{2}(L / K)$ is divisible by $n$, and that it equals $n$ when $L / K$ is cyclic. We prove the lemma by induction on $[L: K]$.
nodes.statement_short: Divisible by n; equal to n for cyclic; induct on degree

nodes.name: intermediate field
nodes.statement: Because the group $\operatorname{Gal}(L / K)$ is solvable (ANT, 7.59), there exists a Galois extension $K^{\prime} / K$ with $L \supsetneqq K^{\prime} \supsetneqq K$.
nodes.statement_short: Solvability gives an intermediate Galois K'

nodes.name: bound
nodes.statement:
From the exact sequence

$$
0 \rightarrow H^{2}\left(K^{\prime} / K\right) \rightarrow H^{2}(L / K) \rightarrow H^{2}\left(L / K^{\prime}\right)
$$

we see that

$$
\left|H^{2}(L / K)\right| \leq\left|H^{2}\left(K^{\prime} / K\right)\right| \cdot\left|H^{2}\left(L / K^{\prime}\right)\right|=n .
$$
nodes.statement_short: Inflation-restriction bounds |H^2(L/K)| by n

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem III.2.1
nodes.statement: Proof (of Theorem 2.1) From the diagram in the proof of (2.2) we see that, for every finite Galois extension $L$ of $K$, the subgroup $H^{2}(L / K)$ of $H^{2}\left(K^{\mathrm{al}} / K\right)$ is contained in $H^{2}\left(K^{\text {un }} / K\right)$. Since $H^{2}\left(K^{\text {al }} / K\right)=\bigcup H^{2}(L / K)$, this proves that the inflation map $H^{2}\left(K^{\text {un }} / K\right) \rightarrow H^{2}\left(K^{\text {al }} / K\right)$ is an isomorphism. Compose the inverse of this with the invariant map $\operatorname{inv}_{K}: H^{2}\left(K^{\text {un }} / K\right) \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}$ of Theorem 1.7. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: H^2(L/K) lies in the unramified part by Lemma 2.6, so inflation H^2(K^un/K) -> H^2(K^al/K) is an isomorphism; compose with inv_K of Theorem 1.7.

nodes.name: inv_L o Res = [L:K] inv_K (29)

nodes.statement: \operatorname{inv}_{L} \circ \operatorname{Res}=[L: K] \operatorname{inv}_{K} . \tag{29}

nodes.name: inv_K o Cor = inv_L (30)

nodes.statement: \operatorname{inv}_{K} \circ \operatorname{Cor}=\operatorname{inv}_{L} . \tag{30}

nodes.name: Proof of (30)
nodes.statement:
Because Res is surjective (see diagram (28)), to prove this it suffices to show that

$$
\operatorname{inv}_{K} \circ \text { Cor } \circ \operatorname{Res}=\operatorname{inv}_{L} \circ \operatorname{Res} .
$$

But Cor $\circ$ Res $=[L: K]$ by (II, 1.30), and so this is the preceding equality (29).
nodes.statement_short: Res is surjective; Cor o Res = [L:K] reduces (30) to (29).

nodes.name: fundamental class u_{L/K}
nodes.statement:
Let $L$ be a finite Galois extension of $K$ with Galois group $G$. As in the unramified case, we define the fundamental class $u_{L / K}$ of $L / K$ to be the element $u_{L / K}$ of $H^{2}(L / K)$ such that

$$
\operatorname{inv}_{L / K}\left(u_{L / K}\right)=\frac{1}{[L: K]} \bmod \mathbb{Z},
$$

or, equivalently, such that

$$
\operatorname{inv}_{K}\left(u_{L / K}\right)=\frac{1}{[L: K]} \bmod \mathbb{Z} .
$$

nodes.name: Lemma III.2.7 (functoriality of fundamental classes)
assumptions: $L \supset E \supset K$ with $L / K$ finite and Galois
$L \supset E \supset K$ with $L / K$ finite and Galois

nodes.statement: & \operatorname{Res}\left(u_{L / K}\right)=u_{L / E},  \tag{31}
& \operatorname{Cor}\left(u_{L / E}\right)=[E: K] u_{L / K} . \tag{32}
\operatorname{Inf}\left(u_{E / K}\right)=[L: E] u_{L / K} . \tag{33}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.2.7
nodes.statement:
Proof. Consider\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-50_227_916_817_575}\\
On applying the kernel-cokernel lemma (II, A.2) to the rows (and using that the lemma is functorial), we obtain a commutative diagram,\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-50_245_1057_1217_507}\\
Here $H^{2}(E / K)$ is defined to be the kernel of $\operatorname{Res}: H^{2}\left(K^{\mathrm{al}} / K\right) \rightarrow H^{2}\left(K^{\mathrm{al}} / E\right)$. The equality (31) expresses the fact that the second square commutes. When $E / K$ is Galois, the equality (33) expresses the fact that the first square commutes.

Equality (32) follows from comparing

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{inv}_{K}\left(\operatorname{Cor}_{E / K}\left(u_{L / E}\right)\right) & \stackrel{(30)}{=} \operatorname{inv}_{E}\left(u_{L / E}\right)=\frac{1}{[L: E]} \bmod \mathbb{Z} \\
& \operatorname{inv}_{K}\left(u_{L / K}\right)=\frac{1}{[L: K]} \bmod \mathbb{Z} .
\end{aligned}
$$ \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Kernel-cokernel lemma applied to the restriction diagrams gives (31) and (33); (32) follows from (30) by comparing invariants.

nodes.name: kernel-cokernel
nodes.statement:
Consider\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-50_227_916_817_575}\\
On applying the kernel-cokernel lemma (II, A.2) to the rows (and using that the lemma is functorial), we obtain a commutative diagram,\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-50_245_1057_1217_507}\\
Here $H^{2}(E / K)$ is defined to be the kernel of $\operatorname{Res}: H^{2}\left(K^{\mathrm{al}} / K\right) \rightarrow H^{2}\left(K^{\mathrm{al}} / E\right)$. The equality (31) expresses the fact that the second square commutes. When $E / K$ is Galois, the equality (33) expresses the fact that the first square commutes.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the kernel-cokernel lemma to the rows

nodes.statement:
Equality (32) follows from comparing

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{inv}_{K}\left(\operatorname{Cor}_{E / K}\left(u_{L / E}\right)\right) & \stackrel{(30)}{=} \operatorname{inv}_{E}\left(u_{L / E}\right)=\frac{1}{[L: E]} \bmod \mathbb{Z} \\
& \operatorname{inv}_{K}\left(u_{L / K}\right)=\frac{1}{[L: K]} \bmod \mathbb{Z} .
\end{aligned}
$$
nodes.statement_short: (32) by comparing invariants using (30)

nodes.name: Remark III.2.8 (K^x/Nm vs H^2(L/K))
nodes.statement: REMARK 2.8 There are groups $K^{\times} / \operatorname{Nm}\left(L^{\times}\right)$and $H^{2}(L / K)$ attached to every finite extension $L / K$ of local fields. When $L / K$ is cyclic, they are isomorphic, but not otherwise. The first group is always isomorphic to $\operatorname{Gal}(M / K)$, where $M$ is the largest abelian subextension of $L / K$ (see 3.4, 3.5), and the second is always cyclic of order $[L: K]$. Thus, when $L / K$ is abelian but not cyclic, the two groups have the same order but are not isomorphic, and when $L / K$ is not abelian, they have different orders.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem III.3.1
nodes.statement: The pair $\left(G, L^{\times}\right)$satisfies the hypotheses of Tate's theorem (II, 3.11),and so we have proved the following result.
nodes.statement_short: (G, L^x) satisfies the hypotheses of Tate's theorem.

nodes.name: Theorem III.3.1 (cup product with the fundamental class)
nodes.statement_short: Cup product with u_{L/K} gives H_T^r(Gal(L/K),Z) = H_T^{r+2}(Gal(L/K),L^x); for r = -2, G^ab = K^x / Nm L^x.

nodes.name: Tate isomorphism commutes with Res and Cor
nodes.statement: If $L \supset E \supset K$ with $L / K$ Galois, then the homomorphism in the theorem commutes with both Res and Cor.

nodes.name: Proof of compatibility with Res and Cor
nodes.statement:
For example, to prove the statement for Res we must show that

$$
\operatorname{Res}\left(x \cup u_{L / K}\right)=\operatorname{Res}(x) \cup u_{L / E}
$$

for all $x \in H_{T}^{r}\left(\operatorname{Gal}(L / K), L^{\times}\right)$. But a standard property of cup-products (II, 1.39c) is that

$$
\operatorname{Res}\left(x \cup u_{L / K}\right)=\operatorname{Res}(x) \cup \operatorname{Res}\left(u_{L / K}\right),
$$

and so this follows from (31). The proof for Cor is similar.
nodes.statement_short: Res(x cup u) = Res x cup Res u (1.39c) and Res u_{L/K} = u_{L/E} (31).

nodes.name: Tate isomorphism and inflation
nodes.statement:
If $L \supset E \supset K$ with $L / K$ and $E / K$ Galois and $x \in H^{r}\left(\operatorname{Gal}(E / K), E^{\times}\right)$with $r \geq 1$, then

$$
\operatorname{Inf}\left(x \cup u_{E / K}\right)=[L: E] \operatorname{Inf}(x) \cup u_{L / K} .
$$

nodes.name: Proof of compatibility with Inf
nodes.statement: Again, this follows from a standard property of cup-products (1.39e) and the formula (33).

nodes.name: local Artin map phi_{L/K}
nodes.statement:
For $r=-2$, the map in the theorem becomes

$$
\operatorname{Gal}(L / K)^{\mathrm{ab}} \xrightarrow{\simeq} K^{\times} / \mathrm{Nm}_{L / K} L^{\times} .
$$

We denote the inverse map by

$$
\phi_{L / K}: K^{\times} / \mathrm{Nm}_{L / K} L^{\times} \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}(L / K)^{\mathrm{ab}}
$$

and call it the local Artin map, or by $\operatorname{rec}_{L / K}$ and call it the local reciprocity map.

nodes.name: Lemma III.3.2 (Artin map and Res/Cor)
nodes.statement:
Lemma 3.2 Let $L \supset E \supset K$ be local fields with $L / K$ Galois. Then the following diagrams commute:\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-51_242_1144_1763_461}\\
The unmarked vertical arrows are induced by the inclusions $\operatorname{Gal}(L / E) \subset \operatorname{Gal}(L / K)$ and $K \subset E$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.3.2 (to be added)
nodes.statement: Proof. To be added (the second is not really needed). \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Not given.

nodes.name: 3.3 Artin map compatible with quotients
nodes.statement:
3.3 Let $L \supset E \supset K$ be local fields with both $L$ and $E$ Galois over $K$. Then the following diagram commutes:\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-51_207_391_2324_838}\\
The unmarked vertical arrow is induced by the surjection $\sigma \mapsto \sigma \mid E: \operatorname{Gal}(L / K) \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}(E / K)$.

nodes.name: Proof of 3.3
nodes.statement: Proof. This follows directly from the definition of the local Artin map, using (33). ${ }^{3}$ \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: From the definition of the Artin map and (33).

nodes.name: local Artin map phi_K
nodes.statement: In particular, if $L \supset E \supset K$ is a tower of finite abelian extensions of $K$, then $\phi_{L / K}(a) \mid E=\phi_{E / K}(a)$ for all $a \in K^{\times}$, and so we can define $\varphi_{K}: K^{\times} \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{ab}} / K\right)$ to be the homomorphism such that, for every finite abelian extension $L / K, \phi_{K}(a) \mid L=$ $\varphi_{L / K}(a)$.

nodes.name: Theorem III.3.4 (local Artin map)
nodes.statement:
Theorem 3.4 For every local field $K$, there exists a homomorphism (local Artin map)

$$
\phi_{K}: K^{\times} \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{ab}} / K\right)
$$

with the following properties:

\begin{itemize}
  \item[(a)] for every prime element $\pi$ of $K, \phi_{K}(\pi) \mid K^{\mathrm{un}}=\operatorname{Frob}_{K}$;
  \item[(b)] for every finite abelian extension $L$ of $K, \operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(L^{\times}\right)$is contained in the kernel of $a \mapsto \phi_{K}(a) \mid L$, and $\phi_{K}$ induces an isomorphism
$$
\phi_{L / K}: K^{\times} / \operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(L^{\times}\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}(L / K) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: There is phi_K: K^x -> Gal(K^ab/K) sending primes to Frobenius on K^un and inducing K^x/Nm L^x = Gal(L/K) for finite abelian L.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem III.3.4
nodes.statement: Proof. Everything is obvious from the above, except (a), which follows from the fact that, for an unramified extension $L$ of $K, \phi_{L / K}$ agrees with that defined in §1, and so we can apply Proposition 1.9. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: From Theorem 3.1 and the construction; (a) reduces to Proposition 1.9 in the unramified case.

nodes.name: Norm Limitation Theorem
nodes.statement:
Theorem 3.5 (Norm Limitation Theorem) Let $L$ be a finite extension of $K$, and let $E$ be the largest abelian extension of $K$ contained in $L$; then

$$
\operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(L^{\times}\right)=\operatorname{Nm}_{E / K}\left(E^{\times}\right) .
$$
assumptions: $E$ be the largest abelian extension of $K$ contained in $L$

nodes.name: Proof of the Norm Limitation Theorem
nodes.statement:
Proof. Because of the transitivity of the norm map, $\mathrm{Nm}_{L / K}\left(L^{\times}\right)$is a subgroup of $\mathrm{Nm}_{E / K}\left(E^{\times}\right)$. If $L / K$ is Galois, then $\operatorname{Gal}(E / K)=\operatorname{Gal}(L / K)^{\text {ab }}$, and so Theorem 3.1 shows that both norm groups have index $[E: K]$ in $K^{\times}$. This implies that they are equal.

In the general case, we let $L^{\prime}$ be a finite Galois extension of $K$ containing $L$. Let $G=\operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\prime} / K\right)$ and $H=\operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\prime} / L\right)$. Thus:\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-52_377_146_2015_959}

\footnotetext{${ }^{3}$ Hervé Jacquet has pointed out that this doesn't appear to be correct, but that the statement can be proved using Proposition 3.6. I don't know whether it can be proved without using 3.6.
}Then $E$ is the largest subfield of $L^{\prime}$ that is abelian over $K$ and contained in $L$. Therefore, the subgroup of $G$ fixing it is $G^{\prime} \cdot H$, where $G^{\prime}$ is the derived group of $G$. Let $a \in \operatorname{Nm}\left(E^{\times}\right)$. We have to show that $a \in \operatorname{Nm}\left(L^{\times}\right)$. Consider the commutative diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-53_337_322_521_871}\\
The element $\phi_{L^{\prime} / K}(a)$ of $G / G^{\prime}$ maps to 1 in $G / G^{\prime} H$. As $\phi_{L^{\prime} / L}$ is surjective, we see from the diagram that there exists a $b \in L^{\times}$such $\phi_{L^{\prime} / K}(a)=\phi_{L^{\prime} / K}(\operatorname{Nm}(b))$, and hence $a / \operatorname{Nm}(b) \in \operatorname{Nm}\left(L^{\prime \times}\right)$, say, $a / \operatorname{Nm}(b)=\operatorname{Nm}(c)$. Now

$$
a=\operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(b \cdot \operatorname{Nm}_{L^{\prime} / L}(c)\right) \in \operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(L^{\times}\right) .
$$ \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Galois case by comparing indices via Theorem 3.1; general case by passing to a Galois closure and chasing Artin maps.

nodes.name: inclusion
nodes.statement: Because of the transitivity of the norm map, $\mathrm{Nm}_{L / K}\left(L^{\times}\right)$is a subgroup of $\mathrm{Nm}_{E / K}\left(E^{\times}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Transitivity: Nm_L is contained in Nm_E

In the general case, we let $L^{\prime}$ be a finite Galois extension of $K$ containing $L$. Let $G=\operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\prime} / K\right)$ and $H=\operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\prime} / L\right)$. Thus:\\

\footnotetext{${ }^{3}$ Hervé Jacquet has pointed out that this doesn't appear to be correct, but that the statement can be proved using Proposition 3.6. I don't know whether it can be proved without using 3.6.
}Then $E$ is the largest subfield of $L^{\prime}$ that is abelian over $K$ and contained in $L$. Therefore, the subgroup of $G$ fixing it is $G^{\prime} \cdot H$, where $G^{\prime}$ is the derived group of $G$. Let $a \in \operatorname{Nm}\left(E^{\times}\right)$. We have to show that $a \in \operatorname{Nm}\left(L^{\times}\right)$. Consider the commutative diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-53_337_322_521_871}\\
The element $\phi_{L^{\prime} / K}(a)$ of $G / G^{\prime}$ maps to 1 in $G / G^{\prime} H$. As $\phi_{L^{\prime} / L}$ is surjective, we see from the diagram that there exists a $b \in L^{\times}$such $\phi_{L^{\prime} / K}(a)=\phi_{L^{\prime} / K}(\operatorname{Nm}(b))$, and hence $a / \operatorname{Nm}(b) \in \operatorname{Nm}\left(L^{\prime \times}\right)$, say, $a / \operatorname{Nm}(b)=\operatorname{Nm}(c)$. Now

$$
a=\operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(b \cdot \operatorname{Nm}_{L^{\prime} / L}(c)\right) \in \operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(L^{\times}\right) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: General case via a Galois closure L'

nodes.name: Galois closure
nodes.statement: In the general case, we let $L^{\prime}$ be a finite Galois extension of $K$ containing $L$. Let $G=\operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\prime} / K\right)$ and $H=\operatorname{Gal}\left(L^{\prime} / L\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose L' Galois over K containing L

nodes.name: fixing group of E
nodes.statement: Then $E$ is the largest subfield of $L^{\prime}$ that is abelian over $K$ and contained in $L$. Therefore, the subgroup of $G$ fixing it is $G^{\prime} \cdot H$, where $G^{\prime}$ is the derived group of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: E is fixed by G'H

nodes.name: Artin map chase
nodes.statement:
Let $a \in \operatorname{Nm}\left(E^{\times}\right)$. We have to show that $a \in \operatorname{Nm}\left(L^{\times}\right)$. Consider the commutative diagram\\
\includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{e7cfc28e-5737-4710-b4d2-10a47512e540-53_337_322_521_871}\\
The element $\phi_{L^{\prime} / K}(a)$ of $G / G^{\prime}$ maps to 1 in $G / G^{\prime} H$. As $\phi_{L^{\prime} / L}$ is surjective, we see from the diagram that there exists a $b \in L^{\times}$such $\phi_{L^{\prime} / K}(a)=\phi_{L^{\prime} / K}(\operatorname{Nm}(b))$, and hence $a / \operatorname{Nm}(b) \in \operatorname{Nm}\left(L^{\prime \times}\right)$, say, $a / \operatorname{Nm}(b)=\operatorname{Nm}(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Chase phi_{L'/K}(a) through the diagram to find b and c

nodes.name: a is a norm
nodes.statement:
Now

$$
a=\operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(b \cdot \operatorname{Nm}_{L^{\prime} / L}(c)\right) \in \operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(L^{\times}\right) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: a is a norm from L

nodes.name: no classification of nonabelian extensions by norms
nodes.statement: Theorem 3.5 shows that there is no hope of classifying nonabelian extensions of a local field in terms of the norm groups.

nodes.name: Proposition III.3.6 (Artin map via invariants)
nodes.statement:
Proposition 3.6 For every $\chi \in \operatorname{Hom}_{c t s}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})$ and $a \in K^{\times}$,

$$
\chi\left(\phi_{L / K}(a)\right)=\operatorname{inv}_{K}(a \cup \delta \chi) .
$$
nodes.origin_citation: Serre 1962, Annexe to Chapter XI; Serre 1967a, p. 140

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition III.3.6 (reference)
nodes.statement: Proof. See Serre 1962, "Annexe" to Chapter XI, and Serre 1967a, p. 140. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Reference to Serre.

nodes.name: Lemma III.3.7 (Artin map of unramified extensions)
nodes.statement: Lemma 3.7 If $L / K$ is unramified, $\phi_{L / K}$ sends $a \in K^{\times}$to Frob $^{\text {ord }_{K}(a)}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma III.3.7
nodes.statement:
Proof. Recall that $\operatorname{inv}_{K}$ is defined to be the composite

$$
H^{2}\left(G, L^{\times}\right) \xrightarrow{\text { ord }} H^{2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \stackrel{\delta}{\leftarrow} \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{\chi \mapsto \chi(\sigma)} \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z} .
$$

Because of the functoriality of cup-products

$$
\operatorname{ord}(a \cup \delta \chi)=\operatorname{ord}(a) \cup \delta \chi, \quad a \in K^{\times}, \quad \chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})
$$

where, on the left ord denotes the map on $H^{2}$ induced by $\operatorname{ord}_{L}: L^{\times} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$, and on the right it is the map itself. Let $a \in H^{0}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)=K^{\times}$, and let $m=\operatorname{ord}_{L}(a)$. For every $\chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})$, in the above diagram,

$$
a \cup \delta \chi \mapsto \operatorname{ord}(a) \cup \delta \chi \mapsto m \chi \mapsto \chi\left(\sigma^{m}\right), \quad \sigma=\text { Frob },
$$

i.e., $\operatorname{inv}_{K}(a \cup \delta \chi)=\chi\left(\sigma^{m}\right)$. On combining this with the formula in (3.6) we find that

$$
\chi(\phi(\alpha))=\chi\left(\sigma^{\operatorname{ord}(\alpha)}\right)
$$

for all $\chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})$, and so $\phi(\alpha)=\sigma^{\text {ord }(\alpha)}$. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: Compute inv_K(a cup delta chi) = chi(Frob^{ord a}) via functoriality of cup products, then apply Proposition 3.6.

nodes.name: recall inv
nodes.statement:
Recall that $\operatorname{inv}_{K}$ is defined to be the composite

$$
H^{2}\left(G, L^{\times}\right) \xrightarrow{\text { ord }} H^{2}(G, \mathbb{Z}) \stackrel{\delta}{\leftarrow} \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}) \xrightarrow{\chi \mapsto \chi(\sigma)} \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z} .
$$
nodes.statement_short: Recall the definition of inv_K

nodes.name: functoriality
nodes.statement:
Because of the functoriality of cup-products

$$
\operatorname{ord}(a \cup \delta \chi)=\operatorname{ord}(a) \cup \delta \chi, \quad a \in K^{\times}, \quad \chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})
$$

where, on the left ord denotes the map on $H^{2}$ induced by $\operatorname{ord}_{L}: L^{\times} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$, and on the right it is the map itself.
nodes.statement_short: ord(a cup delta chi) = ord(a) cup delta chi

nodes.name: compute invariant
nodes.statement:
Let $a \in H^{0}\left(G, L^{\times}\right)=K^{\times}$, and let $m=\operatorname{ord}_{L}(a)$. For every $\chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})$, in the above diagram,

$$
a \cup \delta \chi \mapsto \operatorname{ord}(a) \cup \delta \chi \mapsto m \chi \mapsto \chi\left(\sigma^{m}\right), \quad \sigma=\text { Frob },
$$

i.e., $\operatorname{inv}_{K}(a \cup \delta \chi)=\chi\left(\sigma^{m}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: inv_K(a cup delta chi) = chi(sigma^m)

nodes.name: apply 3.6
nodes.statement:
On combining this with the formula in (3.6) we find that

$$
\chi(\phi(\alpha))=\chi\left(\sigma^{\operatorname{ord}(\alpha)}\right)
$$

for all $\chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})$, and so $\phi(\alpha)=\sigma^{\text {ord }(\alpha)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3.6 gives phi(a) = sigma^{ord a}

nodes.name: Artin map by duality
nodes.statement: For every character $\chi$ of $G$, we get a character $a \mapsto \operatorname{inv}_{K}(a \cup \delta \chi)$ of $K^{\times}$. By duality we get a map $K^{\times} \rightarrow G$. Proposition 3.6 shows that this map is $\phi_{L / K}: K^{\times} \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}(L / K)$.

nodes.name: Proposition III.4.1 (universal norms are n-th powers)
nodes.statement: Proposition 4.1 Let $K$ be a local field containing a primitive $n$th root of 1 . Any element of $K^{\times}$that is a norm from every cyclic extension of $K$ of degree dividing $n$ is an $n$th power.
assumptions: $K$ be a local field containing a primitive $n$th root of 1
conclusions: Any element of $K^{\times}$that is a norm from every cyclic extension of $K$ of degree dividing $n$ is an $n$th power.

nodes.name: Hilbert symbol (a,b)_p on Q_p
nodes.statement:
For $a, b \in \mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\times}$, define

$$
(a, b)_{p}=\left\{\begin{aligned}
1 & \text { if } z^{2}=a x^{2}+b y^{2} \text { has a nontrivial solution in } \mathbb{Q}_{p} \\
-1 & \text { otherwise }
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

nodes.name: (a,b)_p depends only on classes mod squares
nodes.statement:
Clearly, $(a, b)_{p}$ depends only $a$ and $b$ modulo squares, and so this is a pairing

$$
a, b \mapsto(a, b)_{p}: \mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\times} / \mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\times 2} \times \mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\times} / \mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\times 2} \rightarrow\{ \pm 1\} .
$$

nodes.name: properties of the Hilbert symbol over Q_p
nodes.statement:
Serre shows (ibid. 1.1, 1.2) that this pairing is bi-multiplicative

$$
\left(a a^{\prime}, b\right)_{p}=(a, b)_{p}\left(a^{\prime}, b\right)_{p}, \quad\left(a, b b^{\prime}\right)_{p}=(a, b)_{p}\left(a, b^{\prime}\right)_{p},
$$

symmetric (which in this case is the same as skew-symmetric)

$$
(b, a)_{p}=(a, b)_{p}^{-1}=(a, b)_{p},
$$

and nondegenerate (i.e., the left and right kernels are trivial).

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition III.4.1 for Q_p, n=2
nodes.statement:
Let $a$ be an element of $\mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\times}$that is not a square. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
b \text { is a norm from } \mathbb{Q}_{p}[\sqrt{a}] & \Longleftrightarrow b=z^{2}-a x^{2} \text { has a solution in } \mathbb{Q}_{p} \\
& \Longleftrightarrow z^{2}=a x^{2}+b y^{2} \text { has a nontrivial solution in } \mathbb{Q}_{p} \\
& \Longleftrightarrow(a, b)_{p}=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
b \text { is a norm from } \mathbb{Q}_{p}[\sqrt{a}] \text { for all } a \Longrightarrow(a, b)_{p}=1 \text { for all } a \Longrightarrow b \in \mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\times 2},
$$

by the nondegeneracy of the pairing. This proves the proposition in this case.
nodes.statement_short: b is a norm from Q_p(sqrt a) iff (a,b)_p = 1; nondegeneracy of the Hilbert symbol gives b a square.

nodes.name: norm criterion
nodes.statement:
Let $a$ be an element of $\mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\times}$that is not a square. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
b \text { is a norm from } \mathbb{Q}_{p}[\sqrt{a}] & \Longleftrightarrow b=z^{2}-a x^{2} \text { has a solution in } \mathbb{Q}_{p} \\
& \Longleftrightarrow z^{2}=a x^{2}+b y^{2} \text { has a nontrivial solution in } \mathbb{Q}_{p} \\
& \Longleftrightarrow(a, b)_{p}=1
\end{aligned}
$$
nodes.statement_short: b is a norm from Q_p[sqrt a] iff (a,b)_p = 1

nodes.name: nondegeneracy
nodes.statement:
Thus,

$$
b \text { is a norm from } \mathbb{Q}_{p}[\sqrt{a}] \text { for all } a \Longrightarrow(a, b)_{p}=1 \text { for all } a \Longrightarrow b \in \mathbb{Q}_{p}^{\times 2},
$$

by the nondegeneracy of the pairing. This proves the proposition in this case.
nodes.statement_short: Nondegeneracy gives b in Q_p^{x2}

nodes.name: Hilbert symbol (name)
nodes.statement: Aside 4.2 The map $a, b \mapsto(a, b)_{p}$ is called the Hilbert symbol.

nodes.name: Hilbert product formula

nodes.statement: \prod_{p \leq \infty}(a, b)_{p}=1 . \tag{34}

nodes.name: Hom(G, Z/nZ) (continuous)
nodes.statement: In this subsection, $\operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})$ denotes the group of continuous homomorphisms $G \rightarrow$ $\mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: Step 1: review of periodicity for cyclic groups
nodes.statement:
Recall that for every cyclic group $\bar{G}$ and $\bar{G}$-module $M$, there are isomorphisms

$$
H_{T}^{r}(\bar{G}, M) \rightarrow H_{T}^{r+2}(\bar{G}, M),
$$

which become canonical once one chooses a generator $\sigma$ of $\bar{G}$. More precisely, let $n=(\bar{G}$ : 1) and let $\chi$ be the isomorphism $\bar{G} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}$ sending $\sigma$ to $1 \bmod n$. From the cohomology sequence of

$$
0 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{n} \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow 0,
$$

we obtain a boundary map $\delta: H^{1}(\bar{G}, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H^{2}(\bar{G}, \mathbb{Z})$. The isomorphism

$$
H_{T}^{r}(\bar{G}, M) \rightarrow H_{T}^{r+2}(\bar{G}, M)
$$

is $b \mapsto \delta \chi \cup b$.\\
Now let $K$ be a field (not necessarily local), and let $L / K$ cyclic extension with Galois group $\bar{G}$ (of order $n$ ). When $r=0$ and $M=L^{\times}$, the isomorphism becomes

$$
b \mapsto \delta \chi \cup b: K^{\times} / \operatorname{Nm} L^{\times} \rightarrow H^{2}\left(\bar{G}, L^{\times}\right) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: For cyclic G-bar with generator sigma, periodicity is b -> delta chi cup b; for r = 0 and M = L^x it gives K^x/Nm L^x -> H^2(G-bar, L^x).

nodes.name: symbol (chi,b)' for cyclic extensions
nodes.statement:
For $\chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(\bar{G}, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})$ and $b \in K^{\times}$, define

$$
(\chi, b)^{\prime}=\delta \chi \cup b \in H^{2}\left(\bar{G}, L^{\times}\right) .
$$

nodes.name: (chi,b)' = 0 iff b is a norm
nodes.statement:
The above discussion shows that, if $\chi$ is an isomorphism $\bar{G} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}$, then

$$
(\chi, b)^{\prime}=0 \Longleftrightarrow b \text { is a norm from } L^{\times} .
$$

nodes.name: separable closure K^al and G = Gal(K^al/K)
nodes.statement: Let $K^{\text {al }}$ be a separable algebraic closure of $K$ (thus, simply an algebraic closure if $K$ is perfect $)$, and let $G=\operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{al}} / K\right)$.

nodes.name: mu_n
nodes.statement: Let $\mu_{n}$ be the group of $n$th roots of 1 in $K^{\text {al }}$, regarded as a $G$-module.

nodes.name: Kummer isomorphisms
nodes.statement:
From the cohomology sequence of

$$
0 \longrightarrow \mu_{n} \longrightarrow K^{\mathrm{al} \times} \xrightarrow{x \mapsto x^{n}} K^{\mathrm{al} \times} \longrightarrow 0
$$

and Hilbert's theorem 90 (II, 1.22) we find that

$$
\delta: K^{\times} / K^{\times n} \xrightarrow{\simeq} H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right), \quad H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) \xrightarrow{\simeq} H^{2}\left(G, K^{\text {al× }}\right)_{n} .
$$

Here $H^{2}\left(G, K^{\text {al× }}\right)_{n}$ denotes the group of elements in $H^{2}\left(G, K^{\text {al× }}\right)$ killed by $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Kummer theory: K^x/K^{xn} = H^1(G, mu_n) and H^2(G, mu_n) = H^2(G, K^{al x})_n.

nodes.name: pairing (chi,b) = chi cup delta b
nodes.statement:
Consider the cup-product pairing

$$
\begin{array}{ccccc}
H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}) & \times & H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) & \rightarrow & H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) \\
\text { । } & & \text { ।ʔ } & & \text { ।ʔ } \\
\operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}) & & K^{\times} / K^{\times n} & & H^{2}\left(G, K^{\text {al× }}\right)_{n} .
\end{array}
$$

For $\chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})$ and $b \in K^{\times} / K^{\times n}$, we write $(\chi, b)$ for the image of the pair under the above pairing: $(\chi, b)=\chi \cup \delta b$ (as an element of $H^{2}\left(G, K^{\mathrm{al} \times}\right)$ ).

nodes.name: L_chi
nodes.statement: Let $L_{\chi}$ be the subfield of $K^{\mathrm{al}}$ fixed by $\operatorname{Ker}(\chi)$.

nodes.name: Argument for the norm criterion
nodes.statement:
Thus $L_{\chi}$ is a cyclic extension of $K$ of degree $n$, and $\chi$ induces an isomorphism of its Galois group $\bar{G}$ with $\mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}$. Let $b \in K^{\times}$, and let

$$
(\chi, b)^{\prime}=\delta \chi \cup b \in H^{2}\left(\bar{G}, L^{\times}\right),
$$

as in Step 1. Then

$$
\operatorname{Inf}\left((\chi, b)^{\prime}\right)=(\chi, b) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: (chi,b) is the inflation of (chi,b)'.

nodes.name: (chi,b) = 0 iff b is a norm from L_chi
nodes.statement:
Since the inflation map $H^{2}\left(\bar{G}, L_{\chi}\right) \rightarrow H^{2}\left(G, K^{\text {al× }}\right)$ is injective (see II, 1.36), we deduce that

$$
(\chi, b)=0 \Longleftrightarrow b \text { is a norm from } L_{\chi}^{\times} .
$$
conclusions: (\chi, b)=0 \Longleftrightarrow b \text { is a norm from } L_{\chi}^{\times} .

nodes.name: local pairing (chi,b) = inv_K(chi cup delta b)
nodes.statement:
For $\chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}) \simeq H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})$ and $b \in K^{\times} / K^{\times n} \simeq H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right)$, we now define

$$
(\chi, b)=\operatorname{inv}_{K}(\chi \cup \delta b) \in \frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z} .
$$

Thus, we have a canonical pairing

$$
\chi, b \mapsto(\chi, b): H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}) \times H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) \rightarrow H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) \simeq \frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z} .
$$

nodes.name: Proposition III.4.3 (left kernel is zero)
nodes.statement: Proposition 4.3 The left kernel of this pairing is zero.
conclusions: The left kernel of this pairing is zero.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition III.4.3
nodes.statement:
Proof. Let $\chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})$; we have to show that if $(\chi, b)=0$ for all $b \in K^{\times} / K^{\times n}$, then $\chi=0$.

Recall that the composite of the local Artin map $\phi_{K}: K^{\times} \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{ab}} / K\right)$ with

$$
\tau \mapsto \tau \mid L: \operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{ab}} / K\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}(L / K)
$$

is surjective for every finite extension $L$ of $K$ contained in $K^{\mathrm{ab}}$. This implies that the image of $\phi_{K}$ is dense in $\operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{ab}} / K\right)$. Recall (3.6) that, for $b \in K^{\times}$,

$$
\left(\chi, b \bmod K^{\times n}\right)=\chi\left(\phi_{K}(b)\right) .
$$

Because $\chi$ is continuous, if it is zero on $\phi_{K}\left(K^{\times}\right)$, then it is zero on the whole of $\operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{ab}} / K\right) . \square$
nodes.statement_short: (chi, b) = chi(phi_K(b)) and phi_K has dense image, so a continuous chi vanishing on it is zero.

nodes.name: goal
nodes.statement: Let $\chi \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})$; we have to show that if $(\chi, b)=0$ for all $b \in K^{\times} / K^{\times n}$, then $\chi=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Show chi = 0 if (chi, b) = 0 for all b

nodes.name: dense image
nodes.statement:
Recall that the composite of the local Artin map $\phi_{K}: K^{\times} \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{ab}} / K\right)$ with

$$
\tau \mapsto \tau \mid L: \operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{ab}} / K\right) \rightarrow \operatorname{Gal}(L / K)
$$

is surjective for every finite extension $L$ of $K$ contained in $K^{\mathrm{ab}}$. This implies that the image of $\phi_{K}$ is dense in $\operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{ab}} / K\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: phi_K has dense image

nodes.name: recall 3.6
nodes.statement:
Recall (3.6) that, for $b \in K^{\times}$,

$$
\left(\chi, b \bmod K^{\times n}\right)=\chi\left(\phi_{K}(b)\right) .
$$
nodes.statement_short: (chi, b) = chi(phi_K(b))

nodes.name: continuity
nodes.statement: Because $\chi$ is continuous, if it is zero on $\phi_{K}\left(K^{\times}\right)$, then it is zero on the whole of $\operatorname{Gal}\left(K^{\mathrm{ab}} / K\right) . \square$
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of chi

nodes.name: H^2(G, mu_n (x) mu_n) = mu_n
nodes.statement:
Now assume that $K$ contains a primitive $n$th root of 1 . Thus, $\mu_{n} \approx \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}$ as a $G$ -module (the isomorphism depends on the choice of a primitive $n$th root of 1 ). In particular, $\mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n} \approx \mu_{n}$, and so $H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n}\right) \approx H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right)$ (noncanonically). There is a canonical isomorphism

$$
H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) \otimes \mu_{n} \xrightarrow{\simeq} H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n}\right),
$$

which can be defined as $x, y \mapsto x \cup y$. On combining this with the isomorphism $H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) \rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z}$ given by the invariant map, we obtain an isomorphism

$$
H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n}\right) \simeq \mu_{n} .
$$

nodes.name: Hilbert symbol (a,b)
Theorem III.4.4 (properties of the Hilbert symbol)
nodes.statement:
Theorem 4.4 The Hilbert symbol has the following properties.

\begin{itemize}
  \item[(a)] It is bi-multiplicative, i.e.,
$$
\left(a a^{\prime}, b\right)=(a, b)\left(a^{\prime}, b\right), \quad\left(a, b b^{\prime}\right)=(a, b)\left(a, b^{\prime}\right) .
$$
  \item[(b)] It is skew-symmetric, i.e.,
$$
(b, a)=(a, b)^{-1} .
$$
  \item[(c)] It is nondegenerate, i.e.,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& (a, b)=1 \text { for all } b \in K^{\times} / K^{\times n} \Longrightarrow a \in K^{\times n}, \\
& (a, b)=1 \text { for all } a \in K^{\times} / K^{\times n} \Longrightarrow b \in K^{\times n} .
\end{aligned}
$$
  \item[(d)] $(a, b)=1$ if and only if $b$ is a norm from $K[\sqrt[n]{a}]$.
nodes.statement_short: The Hilbert symbol is bimultiplicative, skew-symmetric, nondegenerate, and (a,b) = 1 iff b is a norm from K[a^{1/n}].

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem III.4.4
nodes.statement:
Proof. Statements (a) and (b) are immediate from the definition of the Hilbert symbol in terms of cup-products.

We next prove (c). Choose an $n$th root of 1 , and use it to define isomorphisms $\mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow$ $\mu_{n}$ and $\mu_{n} \rightarrow \mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n}$. The diagram defined by these maps,

$$
\begin{array}{ccccc}
H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) & \times & H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) & \rightarrow & H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n}\right) \\
\uparrow & & \| & & \uparrow \\
H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}) & \times & H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) & \rightarrow & H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right),
\end{array}
$$

commutes. By Proposition 4.3, the left kernel of the lower pairing is zero. Hence, the left kernel of the upper pairing is also zero, which, by skew-symmetry, implies that the right kernel is zero.

Finally, we prove (d). Assume (for simplicity), that $K[\sqrt[n]{a}]$ has degree $n$ over $K$. Choose a primitive $n$th root $\zeta$ of 1. Then $K[\sqrt[n]{a}]$ is cyclic of degree $n$ over $K$, and its Galois group is generated by the map $\sigma$ sending $\sqrt[n]{a}$ to $\zeta \sqrt[n]{a}$. With this choice of $\zeta$, $a \in K^{\times} / K^{\times n}$ corresponds to the element of $\chi_{a} \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})$ sending $\sigma$ to $1 \bmod$ $n \mathbb{Z}$. As $K[\sqrt[n]{a}]=L_{\chi_{a}}$, (d) follows from the boxed formula above. \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: (a),(b) from cup products; (c) from Proposition 4.3 and skew-symmetry; (d) from the norm criterion for L_chi.

nodes.name: (a)-(c)
nodes.statement:
Statements (a) and (b) are immediate from the definition of the Hilbert symbol in terms of cup-products.

We next prove (c). Choose an $n$th root of 1 , and use it to define isomorphisms $\mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow$ $\mu_{n}$ and $\mu_{n} \rightarrow \mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n}$. The diagram defined by these maps,

$$
\begin{array}{ccccc}
H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) & \times & H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) & \rightarrow & H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n}\right) \\
\uparrow & & \| & & \uparrow \\
H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}) & \times & H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) & \rightarrow & H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right),
\end{array}
$$

commutes. By Proposition 4.3, the left kernel of the lower pairing is zero. Hence, the left kernel of the upper pairing is also zero, which, by skew-symmetry, implies that the right kernel is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Nondegeneracy

nodes.name: comparison diagram
nodes.statement:
Choose an $n$th root of 1 , and use it to define isomorphisms $\mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow$ $\mu_{n}$ and $\mu_{n} \rightarrow \mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n}$. The diagram defined by these maps,

$$
\begin{array}{ccccc}
H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) & \times & H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) & \rightarrow & H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n}\right) \\
\uparrow & & \| & & \uparrow \\
H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}) & \times & H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) & \rightarrow & H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right),
\end{array}
$$

commutes.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the Hilbert pairing with the pairing of Step 3

nodes.name: apply 4.3
nodes.statement: By Proposition 4.3, the left kernel of the lower pairing is zero. Hence, the left kernel of the upper pairing is also zero, which, by skew-symmetry, implies that the right kernel is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 4.3 and skew-symmetry

nodes.name: (d)
nodes.statement: Finally, we prove (d). Assume (for simplicity), that $K[\sqrt[n]{a}]$ has degree $n$ over $K$. Choose a primitive $n$th root $\zeta$ of 1. Then $K[\sqrt[n]{a}]$ is cyclic of degree $n$ over $K$, and its Galois group is generated by the map $\sigma$ sending $\sqrt[n]{a}$ to $\zeta \sqrt[n]{a}$. With this choice of $\zeta$, $a \in K^{\times} / K^{\times n}$ corresponds to the element of $\chi_{a} \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})$ sending $\sigma$ to $1 \bmod$ $n \mathbb{Z}$. As $K[\sqrt[n]{a}]=L_{\chi_{a}}$, (d) follows from the boxed formula above.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition III.4.1
nodes.statement: Proof (of Proposition 4.1) We can deduce Proposition 4.1 from Theorem 4.4 by the same argument as in the case $K=\mathbb{Q}_{p}, n=2$, namely, if $b$ is a norm from $K[\sqrt[n]{a}]$ for all $a$, then $(a, b)=1$ for all $a$ (by 4.4d), and hence $b \in K^{\times n}$ (by 4.4c). \(\square\)
nodes.statement_short: If b is a norm from every K[a^{1/n}] then (a,b) = 1 for all a by 4.4(d), so b is an n-th power by 4.4(c).

nodes.name: Remark III.4.5 (Hilbert symbol and Artin map)
nodes.statement:
REMARK 4.5 The Hilbert symbol is related to the local Artin map by the formula

$$
\phi_{K}(b)\left(a^{\frac{1}{n}}\right)=(a, b) a^{\frac{1}{n}} .
$$

Note that Galois theory tells us that, for every $\tau \in \operatorname{Gal}\left(K\left[a^{\frac{1}{n}}\right] / K\right), \tau a^{\frac{1}{n}}=\zeta a^{\frac{1}{n}}$ for some $n$th root of one $\zeta$ (remember, we are assuming that $K$ contains the $n$th roots of 1 ), and so the point of the formula is that roots of 1 are the same. The proof of the formula is an exercise in cup-products, starting from Proposition 3.6.(a)

nodes.name: Remark III.4.6 (duality)
nodes.statement:
REMARK 4.6 The existence theorem will show that $\phi_{K}$ defines an isomorphism $K^{\times} / K^{\times n} \rightarrow$ $\operatorname{Gal}(L / K)$, where $L / K$ is the largest abelian extension of $K$ of exponent $n$ (without the existence theorem we know only that the map is surjective). Clearly, $\operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})=$ $\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Gal}(L / K), \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})$, which is the dual of $\operatorname{Gal}(L / K)$. Thus, $K^{\times} / K^{\times n}$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z})$ have the same order. This shows that the pairing in Step 2,

$$
H^{1}(G, \mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}) \times H^{1}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) \rightarrow H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) \simeq \frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z}
$$

is nondegenerate. More generally, for every finite $G$-module $M$, the cup-product pairing

$$
H^{r}(G, M) \times H^{2-r}(G, \check{M}) \rightarrow H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) \simeq \frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z}
$$

is nondegenerate - here $\check{M}=\operatorname{Hom}\left(M, \mu_{n}\right)$. This duality theorem was proved by Poitou and Tate in the early 1950s, and was a starting point for the theorems in my book "Arithmetic Duality Theorems". Note that it implies that $H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n} \otimes \mu_{n}\right) \simeq\left(\mu_{n}\right)_{G}$.

nodes.name: Poitou-Tate local duality
nodes.statement:
More generally, for every finite $G$-module $M$, the cup-product pairing

$$
H^{r}(G, M) \times H^{2-r}(G, \check{M}) \rightarrow H^{2}\left(G, \mu_{n}\right) \simeq \frac{1}{n} \mathbb{Z} / \mathbb{Z}
$$

is nondegenerate - here $\check{M}=\operatorname{Hom}\left(M, \mu_{n}\right)$.

nodes.name: Remark III.4.7 (Hilbert symbol and central simple algebras)
nodes.statement: Remark 4.7 The Hilbert symbol has an interpretation in terms of central simple algebras (see the next chapter). For $a, b \in K^{\times}$and $\zeta$ a primitive $n$th root of 1 , define $A(a, b ; \zeta)$ to be the $K$-algebra with generators $i$ and $j$ satisfying the relations $i^{n}=a, j^{n}=b$, and $i j=\zeta j i$. Then, $(a, b)_{v}$ is the class in $\operatorname{Br}(K)_{n}$ represented by $A(a, b ; \zeta)$. Note that for $n=2$, we recover the quaternion algebra $H(a, b)$.

nodes.name: Remark III.4.8 (product formula in general)
nodes.statement:
Remark 4.8 The Hilbert symbol

$$
(,): K^{\times} / K^{\times n} \times K^{\times} / K^{\times n} \rightarrow \mu_{n}
$$

is defined also for $K=\mathbb{R}$ and $n=2$. Moreover, the product formula (34) holds for all number fields and all $n$ (see V, 5.4 below).

nodes.name: norm group
nodes.statement: Recall that a subgroup $N$ of $K^{\times}$is a norm group if there is a finite abelian extension $L / K$ such that $\operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(L^{\times}\right)=N$.

nodes.name: norm groups are open of finite index
nodes.statement: Because $K^{\times} / N \xrightarrow{\simeq} \operatorname{Gal}(L / K)$, such a group $N$ is of finite index in $K^{\times}$and hence open (I, 1.3).

nodes.name: Existence Theorem
nodes.statement: Theorem 5.1 (Existence Theorem) Every open subgroup of finite index in $K^{\times}$is a norm group.
assumptions: Every open subgroup of finite index in $K^{\times}$

nodes.name: Remark III.5.2 (abstract existence axioms)
Proof of the Existence Theorem
nodes.statement:
Proof of Theorem 5.1\\
Step 1. For all finite extensions $L / K$, the norm map $L^{\times} \rightarrow K^{\times}$has closed image and compact kernel.

Proof. Since the image has finite index, it is open (see I, 1.3), and hence closed. The kernel is closed, and the equality

$$
\operatorname{ord}_{L}(\operatorname{Nm}(a))=[L: K] \operatorname{ord}_{L}(a)=f \cdot \operatorname{ord}_{K}(a),
$$

shows that it contained in $U_{K}$, which is compact. \(\square\)

Let $D_{K}=\bigcap \mathrm{Nm}_{L / K}\left(L^{\times}\right)$, where $L$ runs over the finite extensions of $K$ (or only the finite abelian extensions - after Theorem 3.5, it is the same).

Step 2. For any finite extension $K^{\prime} / K, \operatorname{Nm}_{K^{\prime} / K} D_{K^{\prime}}=D_{K}$.\\
Proof. Let $a \in D_{K}$, and consider the sets

$$
\operatorname{Nm}_{L / K^{\prime}} L^{\times} \cap \operatorname{Nm}_{K^{\prime} / K}^{-1}(a)
$$

for $L / K^{\prime}$ finite. They are compact and nonempty, and any two contain a third. Therefore their intersection is nonempty (pointset topology). An element in the intersection lies in $D_{K^{\prime}}$ and has norm $a$. \(\square\)

Step 3. The group $D_{K}$ is divisible.\\
Proof. Let $n>1$ be an integer - we have to show that $n D_{K}=D_{K}$. Let $a \in D_{K}$. For each finite extension $L$ of $K$ containing a primitive $n$th root of 1, consider the set

$$
E(L)=\left\{b \in K^{\times} \mid b^{n}=a, \quad b \in \operatorname{Nm}_{L / K} L^{\times}\right\} .
$$

It is nonempty: $a=\operatorname{Nm}_{L / K} a^{\prime}$ for some $a^{\prime} \in D_{L}$; according to Proposition 4.1, $a^{\prime}=c^{n}$ for some $c \in L$, and

$$
\operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}(c)^{n}=\operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}\left(a^{\prime}\right)=a ;
$$

therefore $b \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \operatorname{Nm}_{L / K}(c) \in E(L)$. Moreover, $E\left(L \cdot L^{\prime}\right) \subset E(L) \cap E\left(L^{\prime}\right)$. Since each set is finite, their intersection is nonempty. An element in their intersection lies in $D_{K}$ and has $n$th power $a$. \(\square\)

Step 4. $D_{K}=\{1\}$. [Actually, we don't use this here.]\\
Proof. Choose a prime element of $K$. Let $V_{m, n}=U^{(m)} \times \pi^{n \mathbb{Z}}$. Then $V_{m, n}$ is an (open) subgroup of finite index in $K^{\times}$, and therefore contains $D_{K}$. Now $D_{K} \subset \bigcap_{m, n} V_{m, n}=$ $\{1\}$. \(\square\)

Step 5. Every subgroup $I$ of finite index in $K^{\times}$that contains $U_{K}$ is a norm subgroup.\\
Proof. Since $\operatorname{ord}_{K}: K^{\times} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ is surjective with kernel $U_{K}$, the subgroups $I$ in question are the subgroups of $K^{\times}$of the form $\operatorname{ord}_{K}^{-1}(n \mathbb{Z}), n \geq 1$. Let $K_{n}$ be the unramified extension of $K$ of degree $n$. Then $\operatorname{Nm}_{K_{n} / K}\left(K_{n}^{\times}\right)$is a subgroup of $K^{\times}$containing $U_{K}$ (see 1.2) with image $n \mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Z}$. The statement follows. \(\square\)

We now prove the theorem. Let $\mathcal{N}$ be the set of norm groups in $K^{\times}$, so that $D_{K}=$ $\bigcap_{N \in \mathcal{N}} N$. Let $I$ be a subgroup of $K^{\times}$of finite index. Because $D_{K}$ is divisible, $I \supset D_{K}$, and so $I \supset \bigcap_{N \in \mathcal{N}} N \supset \bigcap_{N \in \mathcal{N}}\left(N \cap U_{K}\right)$. Therefore the sets $\left(N \cap U_{K}\right) \backslash I$ have empty intersection. As they are compact some finite subfamily has empty intersection, i.e., for\\
some finite subset $\mathcal{S}$ of $\mathcal{N}, I \supset \bigcap_{N \in \mathcal{S}}\left(N \cap U_{K}\right)$. As any two of the sets $N \cap U_{K}$ contains a third, this implies that $I \supset N \cap U_{K}$ for some $N$.

Fix a norm group $N$ such that $N \cap U_{K} \subset I$. I claim that $I$ contains

$$
N \cap\left(U_{K} \cdot(N \cap I)\right) .
$$

Indeed, every element of the intersection is of the form $a b, a \in U_{K}, b \in N \cap I, a b \in N$. The last two statements imply that $a \in N$. Hence $a \in N \cap U_{K} \subset I$, and so $a b \in I$.

Now $N \cap I$ is of finite index in $K^{\times}$because both $N$ and $I$ are and $K^{\times} / N \cap I$ injects into $\left(K^{\times} / N\right) \times\left(K^{\times} / I\right)$. Hence $U_{K} \cdot(N \cap I)$ is a subgroup of finite index in $K^{\times}$containing $U_{K}$, and so is a norm group (Step 5). Now $N \cap\left(U_{K} \cdot(N \cap I)\right)$, being the intersection of two norm groups, contains a norm group. Therefore, $I$ contains a norm group, which implies that it is a norm group.
nodes.statement_short: The universal norm group D_K is divisible (via Proposition 4.1), so every finite-index subgroup contains it; compactness then gives N cap U_K in I, and combining with unramified norm groups shows I is a norm group.
